chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot County, Maryland. I have no reliable knowledge of my own age, since I have never seen any official record of it. Most slaves know as little about their ages as horses do about theirs, and nearly every master I knew of wanted to keep them that ignorant. I cannot remember ever meeting a slave who could name his birthday. The closest they ever come is something like planting-time, harvest-time, cherry-time, spring, or fall. Not knowing my own age troubled me even as a child. The white children could state theirs, and I could not see why I should be denied the same privilege. I was not allowed to ask my master about it. He considered any such question from a slave improper, impertinent, and a sign of a restless spirit. My nearest estimate puts me now at between twenty-seven and twenty-eight, which I reach because I once heard my master say, sometime in 1835, that I was about seventeen.
My mother's name was Harriet Bailey. She was the daughter of Isaac and Betsey Bailey, both of them colored and quite dark. Her complexion was darker than either my grandmother's or my grandfather's.

My father was a white man. Everyone I ever heard speak of my parentage took that for granted. It was also whispered that my master was my father, but I know nothing about whether that was true; I was kept from any means of finding out. My mother and I were separated while I was still an infant, before I ever knew her as my mother. In the part of Maryland I escaped from, it was common practice to separate children from their mothers very early. Often, before a child had even reached its first year, the mother would be taken away and hired out to a farm some distance off, and the child left in the care of an old woman too old for field work. I do not know why this was done, unless it was to keep the child from forming any attachment to its mother, and to dull and destroy the mother's natural love for her child. That is the unavoidable result.

In my whole life I saw my mother, knowing her as my mother, no more than four or five times, and each of those visits was very brief and came at night. She had been hired out to a Mr. Stewart, who lived about twelve miles from my home. She made her visits to me at night, walking the entire distance on foot after finishing a full day's labor. She was a field hand, and any slave not in the field by sunrise was whipped for it, unless granted special permission by the master—a permission rarely given, and one that earned whoever granted it the flattering name of a kind master. I do not recall ever seeing my mother in daylight. She was only with me at night. She would lie down with me and get me to sleep, but long before I woke she was gone. Very little ever passed between us in words. Death soon ended the little we could have while she lived, and ended her hardship and suffering along with it. She died when I was about seven, on one of my master's farms near Lee's Mill. I was not allowed to be present during her illness, at her death, or at her burial. She was gone long before I learned anything of it. Having never really known her soothing presence or her tender, watchful care, I received the news of her death with much the same feeling I would have had at the death of a stranger.

Taken away so suddenly, she left me without the slightest hint of who my father was. The whispered claim that my master was my father may or may not be true; but true or false, it matters little to my point, while the plain and hateful fact remains that slaveholders have decreed, and established by law, that the children of enslaved women shall in every case inherit the condition of their mothers. The purpose of this is obvious enough: to serve the slaveholders' own lusts and to make the indulgence of their wicked desires profitable as well as pleasurable. For by this cunning arrangement the slaveholder, in more than a few cases, stands to his slaves as both master and father.

I know of such cases, and it is worth noting that these slaves always suffer greater hardships and have more to contend with than the others. To begin with, they are a constant offense to their mistress. She is forever ready to find fault with them; they can seldom do anything that pleases her; and she is never better satisfied than when she sees them under the lash—especially when she suspects her husband of showing his mulatto children favors he withholds from his black slaves. To spare his white wife's feelings, the master is often forced to sell this class of his slaves; and cruel as it may strike anyone for a man to sell his own children to dealers in human flesh, it is frequently the more humane course for him to take. For unless he does, he must either whip them himself or stand by and watch one white son tie up his own brother—only a few shades darker than himself—and lay the bloody lash on his bare back; and if the father objects with even a word, it is set down to parental favoritism and only makes a bad matter worse, both for himself and for the slave he would protect and defend.

Every year brings multitudes of this class of slaves. It was surely an awareness of this fact that led one great Southern statesman to predict that slavery would fall by the inevitable laws of population. Whether or not that prophecy is ever fulfilled, it is plain that a very different-looking class of people is now growing up in the South and being held in slavery—people quite unlike those first brought to this country from Africa; and if their increase does no other good, it will at least undo the force of the argument that God cursed Ham, and that American slavery is therefore right. If only the direct descendants of Ham may scripturally be enslaved, then slavery in the South must soon become unscriptural, for thousands are born into the world every year who, like me, owe their existence to white fathers—and most often to fathers who are also their masters.

I have had two masters. The first was named Anthony—I do not remember his first name. He was usually called Captain Anthony, a title he had acquired, I assume, by sailing a craft on the Chesapeake Bay. He was not considered a wealthy slaveholder. He owned two or three farms and about thirty slaves, all under the charge of an overseer named Plummer. Mr. Plummer was a miserable drunkard, a foul-mouthed swearer, and a savage brute. He always went armed with a cowskin whip and a heavy club. I have known him to cut and slash the women's heads so horribly that even my master would grow enraged at his cruelty and threaten to whip him if he did not control himself. My master, though, was no humane slaveholder. It took extraordinary barbarity on an overseer's part to disturb him. He was a cruel man, hardened by a long life of slaveholding. At times he seemed to take real pleasure in whipping a slave. I was often awakened at daybreak by the most heart-rending screams of an aunt of mine, whom he used to tie up to a joist and whip across her bare back until she was literally covered in blood. No words, no tears, no prayers from his bloodied victim could move his iron heart from its bloody purpose. The louder she screamed, the harder he whipped; and where the blood ran fastest, there he whipped longest. He would whip her to make her scream and whip her to make her hush, and only when overcome by exhaustion would he stop swinging the blood-clotted cowskin. I remember the first time I ever witnessed this horrible exhibition. I was only a child, but I remember it well, and I will never forget it as long as I remember anything. It was the first of a long series of such outrages that I was doomed to witness and to take part in. It struck me with terrible force. It was the blood-stained gate, the entrance into the hell of slavery, through which I was about to pass. It was a most terrible spectacle, and I wish I could put on paper the feelings with which I watched it.

This took place very soon after I went to live with my old master, and it came about as follows. Aunt Hester had gone out one night—where or for what, I do not know—and happened to be away when my master wanted her. He had ordered her not to go out in the evenings, and had warned her that she must never let him catch her in the company of a certain young man who was courting her, a slave belonging to Colonel Lloyd. The young man's name was Ned Roberts, generally called Lloyd's Ned. Why my master was so possessive of her may safely be left to the imagination. She was a woman of noble figure and graceful proportions, with very few equals and even fewer superiors in appearance among the women, colored or white, of our neighborhood.

Aunt Hester had not only disobeyed his orders by going out, but had been found in the company of Lloyd's Ned—and that, I gathered from what he said while whipping her, was the chief offense. Had he been a man of decent morals himself, he might have been thought interested in protecting my aunt's innocence; but anyone who knew him would never suspect him of such virtue. Before he began whipping her, he took her into the kitchen and stripped her from neck to waist, leaving her neck, shoulders, and back entirely bare. He then told her to cross her hands, cursing her with a vile name as he did so. After she crossed them, he tied them with a strong rope and led her to a stool beneath a large hook that had been fixed in the joist for the purpose. He made her stand on the stool and tied her hands to the hook. Now she stood just as he wanted her, her arms stretched up at full length so that she was forced onto the tips of her toes. Then he said to her, “Now, you cursed wretch, I'll teach you to disobey my orders!” and after rolling up his sleeves, he began to lay on the heavy cowskin. Soon the warm red blood was dripping to the floor, amid her heart-rending screams and his horrid curses. I was so terrified and horror-struck by the sight that I hid myself in a closet and dared not venture out until long after the bloody business was over. I expected my own turn would come next. It was all new to me; I had never seen anything like it before. I had always lived with my grandmother on the outskirts of the plantation, where she was set to raise the children of the younger women, so that until then I had been kept away from the bloody scenes that so often took place on the plantation.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: My master’s family consisted of two sons, Andrew and Richard; one daughter, Lucretia; and her husband, Captain Thomas Auld. They all lived together in one house, on the home plantation of Colonel Edward Lloyd. My master was Colonel Lloyd’s clerk and superintendent—what you might call the overseer of the overseers. I spent two years of my childhood on this plantation, in my old master’s family. It was here that I witnessed the bloody event I described in the first chapter; and since this plantation was where I formed my first impressions of slavery, I will describe it, and describe slavery as it existed there. The plantation lies about twelve miles north of Easton, in Talbot county, on the border of Miles River. Its main crops were tobacco, corn, and wheat. These were grown in great abundance, so that, with the produce of this and the other farms he owned, my master was able to keep a large sloop almost constantly busy carrying them to market in Baltimore. This sloop was named Sally Lloyd, in honor of one of the colonel’s daughters. My master’s son-in-law, Captain Auld, was the captain of the vessel, which was otherwise crewed by the colonel’s own slaves. Their names were Peter, Isaac, Rich, and Jake. The other slaves regarded them very highly and looked upon them as the privileged ones of the plantation; for in the eyes of the slaves it was no small thing to be allowed to see Baltimore.

Colonel Lloyd kept three to four hundred slaves on his home plantation, and owned a great many more on the neighboring farms that belonged to him. The farms nearest to the home plantation were named Wye Town and New Design. “Wye Town” was under the supervision of a man named Noah Willis. New Design was under the supervision of a Mr. Townsend. The overseers of these and all the other farms—more than twenty in all—took their advice and direction from the managers of the home plantation. This was the great center of business. It was the seat of government for all twenty farms. Every dispute among the overseers was settled here. If a slave was convicted of any serious offense, became unmanageable, or showed a determination to run away, he was brought here at once, severely whipped, put aboard the sloop, carried to Baltimore, and sold to Austin Woolfolk, or to some other slave-trader, as a warning to the slaves who remained.

Here, too, the slaves of all the other farms received their monthly allowance of food and their yearly clothing. The men and women slaves received, as their monthly food allowance, eight pounds of pork, or its equivalent in fish, and one bushel of corn meal. Their yearly clothing consisted of two coarse linen shirts, one pair of linen trousers like the shirts, one jacket, one pair of trousers for winter made of coarse negro cloth, one pair of stockings, and one pair of shoes—the whole of which could not have cost more than seven dollars. The allowance for the slave children was given to their mothers, or to the old women who cared for them. The children too young to work in the field were given neither shoes, stockings, jackets, nor trousers; their clothing consisted of two coarse linen shirts a year. When these wore out, they went naked until the next allowance-day. Children from seven to ten years old, both boys and girls, almost naked, could be seen at every season of the year.

The slaves were given no beds, unless one coarse blanket can be counted as a bed, and only the men and women received even those. This, however, is not considered a very great hardship. They suffer less from the lack of beds than from the lack of time to sleep; for when their day’s work in the field is finished, most of them still have their washing, mending, and cooking to do, and have few or none of the ordinary means of doing any of it, so that many of their sleeping hours are spent preparing for the next day in the field. When this is done, old and young, male and female, married and single drop down side by side on one common bed—the cold, damp floor—each covering himself or herself with their miserable blankets; and there they sleep until they are summoned to the field by the driver’s horn. At its sound, all must rise and be off to the field. There can be no lingering; everyone must be at his or her post; and woe to those who do not hear this morning summons to the field. For if they are not awakened by the sense of hearing, they are awakened by the sense of feeling: no age and no sex is shown any mercy. Mr. Severe, the overseer, used to stand by the door of the slave quarters, armed with a large hickory stick and a heavy cowskin whip, ready to whip anyone unlucky enough not to hear, or who for any other reason failed to be ready to start for the field at the sound of the horn.

Mr. Severe was rightly named: he was a cruel man. I have seen him whip a woman until the blood ran for half an hour at a time—and this in the midst of her crying children, who pleaded for their mother’s release. He seemed to take pleasure in displaying his fiendish brutality. On top of his cruelty, he was a foul-mouthed swearer. It was enough to chill the blood and make the hair stand up on an ordinary man just to hear him talk. Scarcely a sentence left his mouth that was not begun or ended with some horrid oath. The field was the place to see his cruelty and profanity. His presence made it both a field of blood and a field of blasphemy. From sunrise until sundown he was cursing, raving, cutting, and slashing among the slaves of the field in the most frightful way. His career was short. He died very soon after I came to Colonel Lloyd’s, and he died as he had lived, uttering, with his dying groans, bitter curses and horrid oaths. The slaves regarded his death as the work of a merciful providence.

Mr. Severe’s place was filled by a Mr. Hopkins. He was a very different man. He was less cruel, less profane, and made less noise than Mr. Severe. His conduct showed no extraordinary displays of cruelty. He whipped, but he seemed to take no pleasure in it. The slaves called him a good overseer.

Colonel Lloyd’s home plantation had the appearance of a country village. All the mechanical work for all the farms was done here. The shoemaking and mending, the blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain-grinding were all performed by the slaves on the home plantation. The whole place had a business-like look quite unlike the neighboring farms. The sheer number of buildings, too, helped give it an advantage over the neighboring farms. The slaves called it the _Great House Farm._ Among the slaves of the out-farms, few privileges were prized more highly than being chosen to run errands at the Great House Farm. In their minds it was associated with greatness. A congressman could not be prouder of his election to a seat in the American Congress than a slave on one of the out-farms would be of being chosen to run errands at the Great House Farm. They saw it as proof of the great confidence their overseers placed in them; and for this reason, as well as a constant desire to be out of the field and away from the driver’s lash, they considered it a high privilege, one worth living carefully to earn. The man who was given this honor most often was called the smartest and most trustworthy fellow. Those competing for this position worked as diligently to please their overseers as office-seekers in the political parties work to please and deceive the people. The same traits of character could be seen in Colonel Lloyd’s slaves as are seen in the slaves of the political parties.

The slaves chosen to go to the Great House Farm to collect the monthly allowance for themselves and their fellow-slaves were especially enthusiastic. On their way there, they would make the dense old woods for miles around echo with their wild songs, which revealed at once the highest joy and the deepest sadness. They would compose and sing as they went along, paying no heed to time or tune. Whatever thought came into their minds came out—if not in the words, then in the sound; and as often in one as in the other. Sometimes they would sing the most sorrowful sentiment in the most joyful tone, and the most joyful sentiment in the most sorrowful tone. Into all their songs they would manage to weave something of the Great House Farm. They did this especially when leaving home. Then they would sing, most exultantly, the following words:—
“I am going away to the Great House Farm! O, yea! O, yea! O!”

They would sing this as a chorus, set to words that to many would seem meaningless gibberish, but which were nevertheless full of meaning to themselves. I have sometimes thought that simply hearing those songs would do more to impress some minds with the horrible nature of slavery than reading whole volumes of philosophy on the subject could do.

While I was a slave, I did not understand the deep meaning of those crude and apparently incoherent songs. I was myself within the circle, so that I neither saw nor heard what those outside of it might see and hear. They told a tale of misery that was then completely beyond my feeble understanding; they were tones loud, long, and deep; they breathed the prayer and complaint of souls overflowing with the bitterest anguish. Every tone was a testimony against slavery, and a prayer to God for deliverance from chains. Hearing those wild notes always lowered my spirits and filled me with an indescribable sadness. I have often found myself in tears while listening to them. Even now, the mere memory of those songs afflicts me; and as I write these lines, a feeling has already found its way down my cheek in the form of a tear. To those songs I trace my first faint idea of the dehumanizing nature of slavery. I can never rid myself of that idea. Those songs still follow me, deepening my hatred of slavery and quickening my sympathy for my brethren in bondage. If anyone wishes to be impressed with the soul-killing effects of slavery, let him go to Colonel Lloyd’s plantation and, on allowance-day, place himself in the deep pine woods, and there let him, in silence, examine the sounds that pass through the chambers of his soul—and if he is not moved by them, it will only be because “there is no flesh in his obdurate heart.”

Since coming to the north, I have often been utterly astonished to find people who could speak of the singing of slaves as evidence of their contentment and happiness. It is impossible to imagine a greater mistake. Slaves sing most when they are most unhappy. The songs of the slave express the sorrows of his heart, and they relieve him only as an aching heart is relieved by its tears. At least, that is my own experience. I have often sung to drown my sorrow, but seldom to express my happiness. Crying for joy, and singing for joy, were both equally rare for me while in the jaws of slavery. The singing of a man cast away on a desolate island might just as fittingly be taken as evidence of contentment and happiness as the singing of a slave; the songs of the one and of the other are prompted by the same emotion.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Colonel Lloyd kept a large, beautifully tended garden that gave nearly full-time work to four men besides the head gardener, Mr. M’Durmond. It was probably the greatest attraction on the place. All through the summer, people traveled from far and wide—from Baltimore, Easton, and Annapolis—just to see it. It was full of fruit of almost every kind, from the hardy northern apple to the delicate southern orange. The garden was also no small source of trouble on the plantation. Its fine fruit was a powerful temptation to the hungry swarms of boys and to the older slaves alike, few of whom had either the virtue or the vice to resist it. Hardly a day went by in summer without some slave taking the lash for stealing fruit. The colonel tried every kind of trick to keep his slaves out of it. The last and most effective was to tar the fence all the way around; after that, if a slave was caught with any tar on him, it was taken as proof enough that he had been in the garden or had tried to get in—and either way the head gardener whipped him severely. The scheme worked: the slaves grew as afraid of tar as of the lash, and seemed to understand that there was no touching tar without being marked by it.

The colonel also kept a magnificent set of carriages and riding gear. His stable and carriage-house looked like one of the big-city livery firms. His horses were of the finest build and noblest bloodlines, and the carriage-house held three splendid coaches, three or four gigs, besides dearborns and barouches in the latest fashion.

Two slaves looked after all of this—old Barney and young Barney, father and son. It was their only job, but it was far from easy, because Colonel Lloyd was more particular about the care of his horses than about anything else. The slightest bit of neglect was unforgivable and brought the harshest punishment down on whoever was responsible. No excuse could protect them if the colonel so much as suspected that his horses had been neglected—and he suspected it often, which made the two Barneys' position a miserable one. They never knew when they were safe from punishment. They were frequently whipped when they least deserved it and escaped when they deserved it most. Everything turned on how the horses looked and on the colonel's own mood when they were brought to him for use. If a horse did not move quickly enough or hold its head high enough, the blame fell on its keepers. It was painful to stand near the stable door and listen to the stream of complaints whenever a horse was led out: “This horse has not had proper attention. He has not been sufficiently rubbed and curried, or he has not been properly fed; his food was too wet or too dry; he got it too soon or too late; he was too hot or too cold; he had too much hay, and not enough of grain; or he had too much grain, and not enough of hay; instead of old Barney's attending to the horse, he had very improperly left it to his son.” To every one of these complaints, however unfair, the slave had to answer not a single word. Colonel Lloyd would not tolerate the least contradiction from a slave; when he spoke, a slave had to stand, listen, and tremble—and that is literally how it was. I have seen Colonel Lloyd force old Barney, a man between fifty and sixty years old, to bare his bald head, kneel on the cold, damp ground, and take more than thirty lashes at a time across his naked, work-worn shoulders. Colonel Lloyd had three sons—Edward, Murray, and Daniel—and three sons-in-law, Mr. Winder, Mr. Nicholson, and Mr. Lowndes. All of them lived at the Great House Farm and enjoyed the privilege of whipping the servants whenever they pleased, from old Barney down to William Wilkes, the coach-driver. I have seen Winder make one of the house-servants stand just far enough off to be reached with the tip of his whip, and raise great welts on the man's back with every stroke.

To describe Colonel Lloyd's wealth would be almost like describing the riches of Job. He kept between ten and fifteen house-servants. He was said to own a thousand slaves, and I think that figure is well within the truth. He owned so many that he did not recognize them when he saw them, and not all the slaves on the out-farms knew him by sight either. The story goes that one day, riding along the road, he met a colored man and spoke to him in the way white men usually addressed colored people on the public roads of the South: “Well, boy, whom do you belong to?” “To Colonel Lloyd,” the slave replied. “Well, does the colonel treat you well?” “No, sir,” came the ready answer. “What, does he work you too hard?” “Yes, sir.” “Well, doesn't he give you enough to eat?” “Yes, sir, he gives me enough, such as it is.”

Having learned where the slave belonged, the colonel rode on, and the man went back to his work, never dreaming that he had been talking with his own master. He thought no more of it, said no more of it, and heard no more of it—until two or three weeks later. Then his overseer informed him that, for having found fault with his master, he was now to be sold to a Georgia trader. He was chained and handcuffed on the spot; and so, without a moment's warning, he was torn away from his family and friends forever, by a hand more pitiless than death. This is the price of telling the truth—the plain, simple truth—in answer to a few plain questions.

It is partly because of facts like these that slaves, when asked about their condition and the character of their masters, almost always say they are content and that their masters are kind. Slaveholders have been known to plant spies among their slaves to find out what they really think and feel about their lot. This has happened often enough that the slaves have adopted the maxim that a still tongue makes a wise head. They keep the truth to themselves rather than face the consequences of speaking it—and in doing so they prove themselves a part of the human family. Whatever they have to say about their masters is usually in the master's favor, especially when they are speaking to a stranger they cannot yet trust. As a slave I was often asked whether I had a kind master, and I don't recall ever once saying no; nor did I feel, in answering that way, that I was telling an outright lie, because I always measured my master's kindness against the standard of kindness set by the slaveholders around us. What is more, slaves are like everyone else and absorb the same prejudices others do. They think their own is better than anyone else's. Many, under the spell of this prejudice, believe their own masters are better than other people's masters—sometimes even when the very reverse is true. It is not unusual for slaves to fall out and quarrel among themselves over whose master is the better man, each insisting on the superior goodness of his own over the rest. And yet, taken one by one, they curse their masters all the same. So it was on our plantation. Whenever Colonel Lloyd's slaves met the slaves of Jacob Jepson, they seldom parted without a quarrel over their masters—Lloyd's slaves arguing that he was the richest, and Mr. Jepson's that he was the smarter and more of a man. Lloyd's slaves would boast that he could buy and sell Jacob Jepson; Jepson's slaves would boast that their master could whip Colonel Lloyd. These arguments almost always ended in a fight between the two sides, and whoever won the fight was supposed to have won the point at issue. They seemed to think that their masters' greatness somehow passed on to them. It was bad enough to be a slave at all; but to be a poor man's slave was held to be a disgrace indeed!

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: Mr. Hopkins stayed only a short while in the position of overseer. I do not know why his time there was so brief, but I suspect he lacked the harshness that would have satisfied Colonel Lloyd. Mr. Hopkins was followed by Mr. Austin Gore, a man who possessed, to a remarkable degree, all the qualities considered essential to what people call a first-rate overseer. Mr. Gore had already served Colonel Lloyd as overseer on one of the out-farms, and he had proven himself worthy of the higher post of overseer on the home plantation, the Great House Farm.

Mr. Gore was proud, ambitious, and relentless. He was cunning, cruel, and unyielding. He was exactly the right man for such a place, and it was exactly the right place for such a man. The position gave full play to all his powers, and he seemed completely at ease in it. He was one of those men who could twist the slightest look, word, or gesture from a slave into insolence, and would punish it as such. No one was permitted to answer him back; no slave was allowed to explain himself, even when he could show he had been wrongly accused. Mr. Gore lived up entirely to the rule laid down by slaveholders—“It is better that a dozen slaves should suffer under the lash than that the overseer should be proven, in front of the slaves, to have been wrong.” It made no difference how innocent a slave might be—it counted for nothing once Mr. Gore had accused him of any offense. To be accused was to be convicted, and to be convicted was to be punished; the one followed the other with unbreakable certainty. The only way to escape punishment was to escape accusation, and few slaves were lucky enough to manage either while Mr. Gore was overseer. He was proud enough to demand the most degrading deference from the slave, yet servile enough to grovel at the feet of his master. He was ambitious enough to be satisfied with nothing less than the highest rank among overseers, and persistent enough to reach the summit of that ambition. He was cruel enough to inflict the harshest punishments, cunning enough to stoop to the lowest tricks, and hardened enough to feel nothing when his conscience reproached him. Of all the overseers, he was the one the slaves dreaded most. His mere presence was painful; his glance threw them into confusion; and his sharp, shrill voice was seldom heard without striking horror and trembling into their ranks.

Mr. Gore was a solemn man, and though young, he made no jokes, said nothing amusing, and rarely smiled. His words matched his looks perfectly, and his looks matched his words. Overseers will sometimes share a witty remark, even with the slaves; not Mr. Gore. He spoke only to give orders, and gave orders only to be obeyed; he was sparing with his words and generous with his whip, never using the first where the second would serve just as well. When he whipped, he seemed to do it out of a sense of duty, with no fear of the consequences. He did nothing reluctantly, however unpleasant the task; he was always at his post and never inconsistent. He never made a promise except to keep it. In a word, he was a man of the most rigid firmness and stone-cold composure.

His savage brutality was matched only by the utter coolness with which he carried out the grossest and most savage acts against the slaves in his charge. Mr. Gore once set out to whip one of Colonel Lloyd’s slaves, a man named Demby. He had given Demby only a few lashes when, to escape the beating, Demby ran and plunged into a creek, standing there with the water up to his shoulders and refusing to come out. Mr. Gore told him that he would call him three times, and that if he did not come out by the third call, he would shoot him. The first call was given. Demby made no reply but held his ground. The second and third calls were given, with the same result. Then Mr. Gore, without consulting or conferring with anyone, and without even giving Demby an extra call, raised his musket to his face, took deadly aim at his standing victim, and in an instant poor Demby was gone. His mangled body sank out of sight, and blood and brains stained the water where he had stood.

A shudder of horror ran through every soul on the plantation, except Mr. Gore. He alone seemed calm and composed. Colonel Lloyd and my old master asked him why he had resorted to this extraordinary measure. His answer, as well as I can remember, was that Demby had become unmanageable. He was setting a dangerous example to the other slaves—one which, if allowed to pass without some such display on his part, would eventually lead to the complete breakdown of all rule and order on the plantation. He argued that if one slave refused to be corrected and escaped with his life, the other slaves would soon follow his example; the result would be the freedom of the slaves and the enslavement of the whites. Mr. Gore’s defense was accepted as satisfactory. He was kept on as overseer of the home plantation. His reputation as an overseer spread far and wide. His horrible crime was not even brought before a court for investigation. It had been committed in the presence of slaves, who of course could neither file a lawsuit nor testify against him; and so the guilty man who carried out one of the bloodiest and foulest murders goes unpunished by justice and uncensured by the community in which he lives. Mr. Gore was living in St. Michael’s, Talbot county, Maryland, when I left there; and if he is still alive, he very likely lives there still; and if so, he is now, as he was then, held in just as high esteem and respect as if his guilty soul had never been stained with his brother’s blood.

I weigh my words carefully when I say this—that killing a slave, or any colored person, in Talbot county, Maryland, is not treated as a crime, either by the courts or by the community. Mr. Thomas Lanman, of St. Michael’s, killed two slaves, one of whom he killed with a hatchet by beating his brains out. He used to brag about committing that awful and bloody deed. I have heard him do it while laughing, saying, among other things, that he was the only one in the neighborhood doing his country any good, and that when others did as much as he had done, we should be rid of “the d——d niggers.”

The wife of Mr. Giles Hicks, who lived only a short distance from where I used to live, murdered my wife’s cousin, a young girl between fifteen and sixteen years of age, mangling her body in the most horrible way, breaking her nose and her breastbone with a stick, so that the poor girl died a few hours later. She was buried at once, but had been in her untimely grave only a few hours before she was dug up and examined by the coroner, who ruled that she had died from a severe beating. The offense for which this girl was murdered was this: she had been put in charge that night of minding Mrs. Hicks’s baby, and during the night she fell asleep, and the baby cried. Having lost her sleep for several nights before, she did not hear the crying. They were both in the room with Mrs. Hicks. Mrs. Hicks, finding the girl slow to get up, leapt from her bed, snatched an oak stick of wood from the fireplace, and with it broke the girl’s nose and breastbone, and so ended her life. I will not say that this most horrible murder produced no stir in the community. It did produce a stir, but not enough to bring the murderess to punishment. A warrant was issued for her arrest, but it was never carried out. So she escaped not only punishment, but even the discomfort of being brought before a court for her horrible crime.

While I am recounting the bloody deeds that took place during my stay on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation, I will briefly tell of another, which happened around the same time as the murder of Demby by Mr. Gore.

Colonel Lloyd’s slaves were in the habit of spending part of their nights and their Sundays fishing for oysters, and in this way they made up for the shortfall in their meager rations. An old man belonging to Colonel Lloyd, while doing this, happened to stray beyond the boundaries of Colonel Lloyd’s land and onto the property of Mr. Beal Bondly. Mr. Bondly took offense at this trespass, and coming down to the shore with his musket, he fired its deadly charge into the poor old man.

Mr. Bondly came over to see Colonel Lloyd the next day—whether to pay him for his property, or to justify what he had done, I do not know. At any rate, this whole fiendish affair was soon hushed up. Very little was said about it at all, and nothing was done. It was a common saying, even among small white boys, that it was worth a half-cent to kill a “nigger” and a half-cent to bury one.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: As for how I was treated while I lived on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation, it was much the same as the other slave children’s. I wasn’t old enough to work in the field, and since there was little to do besides field work, I had a great deal of free time. The most I had to do was drive the cows in at evening, keep the fowls out of the garden, keep the front yard clean, and run errands for my old master’s daughter, Mrs. Lucretia Auld. Most of my free time I spent helping Master Daniel Lloyd find his birds after he had shot them. My connection with Master Daniel was something of an advantage to me. He grew quite attached to me and became a kind of protector. He wouldn’t let the older boys pick on me, and he would share his cakes with me.

My old master seldom whipped me, and I suffered little from anything except hunger and cold. The hunger was bad, but the cold was far worse. Through the hottest summer and the coldest winter, I was kept almost naked—no shoes, no stockings, no jacket, no trousers, nothing on but a coarse tow-linen shirt that reached only to my knees. I had no bed. I would surely have died from the cold if, on the coldest nights, I hadn’t stolen a bag used for carrying corn to the mill. I would crawl inside this bag and sleep there on the cold, damp clay floor, with my head in and my feet sticking out. My feet were so cracked by the frost that the pen I am writing with now could be laid in the gashes.

We were not given regular rations. Our food was coarse cornmeal boiled into what was called _mush_. It was poured into a large wooden tray or trough and set down on the ground. The children were then called, like so many pigs, and like so many pigs they would come and devour the mush—some with oyster shells, others with pieces of shingle, some with their bare hands, and none with spoons. Whoever ate fastest got the most; whoever was strongest claimed the best place; and few ever left the trough satisfied.

I was probably between seven and eight years old when I left Colonel Lloyd’s plantation. I left it with joy. I will never forget the ecstasy with which I received the news that my old master, Anthony, had decided to let me go to Baltimore to live with Mr. Hugh Auld, brother to my old master’s son-in-law, Captain Thomas Auld. I got this news about three days before I left. They were three of the happiest days I ever knew. I spent most of those three days in the creek, washing off the grime of the plantation and getting myself ready to go.

Whatever pride in my appearance this might seem to show was not really mine. I spent the time washing, not so much because I wanted to, but because Mrs. Lucretia had told me I must get every bit of dead skin off my feet and knees before I could go to Baltimore—for the people there were very clean and would laugh at me if I looked dirty. Besides, she was going to give me a pair of trousers, which I could not wear unless I got all the dirt off myself. The thought of owning a pair of trousers was wonderful indeed! It was almost reason enough to make me scrub away not only what pig-drovers would call the mange, but the very skin itself. I went at it in earnest, working for the first time in my life with the hope of a reward.

The bonds that usually tie children to their homes were all loosened in my case. I found nothing hard about leaving. My home held no charm; it was not a home to me; and in parting from it I could not feel that I was leaving behind anything I might have enjoyed by staying. My mother was dead, and my grandmother lived far away, so that I rarely saw her. I had two sisters and one brother who lived in the same house with me, but our early separation from our mother had nearly erased the fact of our kinship from our memories. I looked for a home elsewhere, certain that I would find none I liked less than the one I was leaving. And even if my new home brought hardship, hunger, whipping, and nakedness, I had the consolation that I could not have escaped a single one of them by staying. Having already tasted more than enough of them in my old master’s house, and having endured them there, I naturally concluded that I could endure them anywhere else—and especially in Baltimore. For I felt about Baltimore something like the spirit of the proverb that “being hanged in England is preferable to dying a natural death in Ireland.” I had the strongest desire to see Baltimore. Cousin Tom, though not a fluent speaker, had stirred that desire in me by his eloquent descriptions of the place. I could never point to anything at the Great House, however beautiful or grand, without his having seen something at Baltimore that far surpassed it in both beauty and strength. Even the Great House itself, with all its pictures, was far inferior to many of the buildings in Baltimore. So strong was my desire that I believed satisfying it would fully make up for whatever comforts I lost in the exchange. I left without a single regret, and with the highest hopes for future happiness.

We sailed out of Miles River for Baltimore on a Saturday morning. I remember only the day of the week, because at that time I had no knowledge of the days of the month or the months of the year. As we set sail, I walked to the stern and gave Colonel Lloyd’s plantation what I hoped would be my last look. Then I took my place at the bow of the sloop and spent the rest of the day there, gazing ahead, more interested in what lay in the distance than in anything near at hand or behind me.

That afternoon we reached Annapolis, the capital of the state. We stopped only a few moments, so I had no chance to go ashore. It was the first large town I had ever seen, and though it would look small beside some of our New England factory villages, I thought it a wonderful place for its size—more impressive even than the Great House Farm!

We arrived at Baltimore early on Sunday morning, landing at Smith’s Wharf, not far from Bowley’s Wharf. We had a large flock of sheep on board the sloop, and after helping drive them to Mr. Curtis’s slaughterhouse on Louden Slater’s Hill, I was led by Rich, one of the hands belonging to the sloop, to my new home on Alliciana Street, near Mr. Gardner’s ship-yard, on Fells Point.

Mr. and Mrs. Auld were both at home, and they met me at the door with their little son Thomas, whom I had been given to look after. And there I saw what I had never seen before—a white face glowing with the kindest feelings; it was the face of my new mistress, Sophia Auld. I wish I could describe the rapture that flashed through my soul as I beheld it. It was a new and strange sight to me, lighting up my path with the glow of happiness. Little Thomas was told that here was his Freddy—and I was told to take care of little Thomas. And so I took up the duties of my new home with the most cheering prospect ahead of me.

I look back on my departure from Colonel Lloyd’s plantation as one of the most significant events of my life. It is possible, and even quite likely, that but for the simple circumstance of being moved from that plantation to Baltimore, I would today—instead of sitting here at my own table, enjoying my freedom and the happiness of a home, writing this Narrative—be locked in the galling chains of slavery. Going to live in Baltimore laid the foundation and opened the gateway to all my later good fortune. I have always regarded it as the first clear sign of that kind providence which has watched over me ever since and marked my life with so many favors. The fact that I was the one chosen struck me as somewhat remarkable. There were a number of slave children who might have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore. There were those younger, those older, and those of the same age. I was picked out from among them all—the first, last, and only choice.

I may be thought superstitious, and even egotistical, for regarding this event as a special intervention of divine Providence on my behalf. But I would be false to the earliest stirrings of my soul if I held back the opinion. I would rather be true to myself, even at the risk of being ridiculed by others, than be false and earn my own contempt. From my earliest memory, I trace the beginning of a deep conviction that slavery would not always be able to hold me in its foul embrace; and in the darkest hours of my life as a slave, this living word of faith and spirit of hope never left me, but stayed like ministering angels to cheer me through the gloom. This good spirit was from God, and to him I offer thanksgiving and praise.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: My new mistress turned out to be everything she seemed when I first met her at the door—a woman with the kindest heart and the finest feelings. She had never had a slave under her authority before me, and before her marriage she had supported herself by her own labor. She was a weaver by trade, and because she had devoted herself so steadily to her work, she had been largely spared the blighting, dehumanizing effects of slavery. Her goodness astonished me completely. I hardly knew how to act toward her. She was utterly unlike any other white woman I had ever known. I could not approach her the way I had been taught to approach other white ladies. Everything I had learned early on was useless here. The cringing servility that was usually so valued in a slave did not work when shown to her. It did not win her favor; it seemed to trouble her. She did not think it impudent or disrespectful for a slave to look her in the face. The lowliest slave was put completely at ease in her presence, and no one left without feeling better for having seen her. Her face was made of heavenly smiles, and her voice of quiet music.

But, sadly, this kind heart could not stay kind for long. The deadly poison of unchecked power was already in her hands, and it soon began its hellish work. That cheerful eye, under the influence of slavery, soon turned red with rage; that voice, once all sweet harmony, changed to one of harsh and terrible discord; and that angelic face gave way to the face of a demon.

Very soon after I went to live with Mr. and Mrs. Auld, she kindly began to teach me the A, B, C. Once I had learned that, she helped me learn to spell words of three or four letters. Right at this point in my progress, Mr. Auld discovered what was happening, and he immediately forbade Mrs. Auld to teach me any further, telling her, among other things, that it was both unlawful and unsafe to teach a slave to read. To quote his own words, he went on to say, “If you give a nigger an inch, he will take an ell. A nigger should know nothing but to obey his master—to do as he is told to do. Learning would _spoil_ the best nigger in the world. Now,” said he, “if you teach that nigger (meaning me) how to read, there would be no keeping him. It would forever unfit him to be a slave. He would at once become unmanageable, and of no value to his master. As to himself, it could do him no good, but a great deal of harm. It would make him discontented and unhappy.” These words sank deep into my heart, stirring up feelings that had been lying dormant, and bringing an entirely new line of thought into being. It was a new and special revelation, explaining the dark and mysterious things my young mind had struggled with—struggled with in vain. I now understood what had been a most baffling difficulty to me: namely, the white man’s power to enslave the black man. It was a tremendous discovery, and I prized it highly. From that moment, I understood the path from slavery to freedom. It was exactly what I needed, and I gained it just when I least expected to. While I was saddened by the thought of losing the help of my kind mistress, I was gladdened by the priceless lesson I had picked up, by the merest accident, from my master. Though I knew how hard it would be to learn without a teacher, I set out with high hope and a firm purpose to learn how to read, whatever the trouble it cost. The very decided way in which he spoke, and tried to impress on his wife the evil consequences of teaching me, only convinced me that he was deeply aware of the truth of what he was saying. It gave me the surest assurance that I could rely with complete confidence on the results he predicted would follow from teaching me to read. What he dreaded most, I desired most. What he loved most, I hated most. What was to him a great evil, to be carefully avoided, was to me a great good, to be diligently pursued; and the very argument he urged so warmly against my learning to read only inspired me with the desire and determination to learn. In learning to read, I owe nearly as much to my master’s bitter opposition as to my mistress’s kindly help. I acknowledge the benefit of both.

I had lived in Baltimore only a short time before I noticed a striking difference in how slaves were treated compared with what I had seen in the country. A city slave is almost a free man compared with a slave on the plantation. He is much better fed and clothed, and he enjoys privileges entirely unknown to the slave on the plantation. There is a trace of decency, a sense of shame, that does much to restrain and check the outbursts of atrocious cruelty so commonly carried out on the plantation. A slaveholder must be desperate indeed to shock the humanity of his non-slaveholding neighbors with the cries of his torn and bleeding slave. Few are willing to take on the disgrace attached to being known as a cruel master; and above all, they would not want to be known as someone who fails to give a slave enough to eat. Every city slaveholder is anxious to be known for feeding his slaves well; and it is only fair to them to say that most of them do give their slaves enough to eat. There are, however, some painful exceptions to this rule. Directly across from us, on Philpot Street, lived Mr. Thomas Hamilton. He owned two slaves. Their names were Henrietta and Mary. Henrietta was about twenty-two years old, Mary about fourteen; and of all the mangled and emaciated creatures I have ever seen, these two were the worst. Anyone who could look on them unmoved must have a heart harder than stone. Mary’s head, neck, and shoulders were literally cut to pieces. I have often felt her head and found it nearly covered with festering sores, caused by the lash of her cruel mistress. I do not know whether her master ever whipped her, but I was an eyewitness to the cruelty of Mrs. Hamilton. I used to be in Mr. Hamilton’s house nearly every day. Mrs. Hamilton would sit in a large chair in the middle of the room, with a heavy cowskin whip always at her side, and scarcely an hour passed during the day without the blood of one of these slaves being drawn. The girls seldom passed her without her saying, “Move faster, you _black gip!_”—and at the same time striking them with the cowskin over the head or shoulders, often drawing blood. She would then say, “Take that, you _black gip!_” and go on, “If you don’t move faster, I’ll move you!” On top of the cruel lashings these slaves endured, they were kept nearly half-starved. They rarely knew what it was to eat a full meal. I have seen Mary fighting with the pigs over the scraps thrown into the street. Mary was kicked and cut to pieces so badly that she was more often called “_pecked_” than by her name.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: I lived with Master Hugh’s family for about seven years. During that time, I managed to learn to read and write. To accomplish this, I had to fall back on all sorts of tricks. I had no regular teacher. My mistress, who had kindly begun to teach me, had—following her husband’s advice and instructions—not only stopped teaching me, but had set herself firmly against my being taught by anyone else. In fairness to my mistress, though, I should say that she did not take up this way of treating me right away. At first she lacked the depravity that was needed to lock me up in mental darkness. She had at least to undergo some training in the use of unaccountable power before she could rise to the task of treating me as though I were a brute.

My mistress was, as I have said, a kind and tender-hearted woman; and in the innocence of her soul she began, when I first came to live with her, to treat me the way she imagined one human being ought to treat another. When she took up the duties of a slaveholder, she did not seem to realize that I stood to her in the position of mere property, and that for her to treat me as a human being was not only wrong but dangerously so. Slavery proved just as harmful to her as it was to me. When I first arrived, she was a pious, warm, and tender-hearted woman. There was no sorrow or suffering for which she had no tear. She had bread for the hungry, clothes for the naked, and comfort for every mourner who came within her reach. Slavery soon showed its power to strip her of these heavenly qualities. Under its influence, her tender heart turned to stone, and her lamblike nature gave way to a tiger-like fierceness. The first step in her downward path was when she stopped teaching me. She now began to put her husband’s principles into practice. In the end she became even more violent in her opposition than her husband himself. She was not content simply to do as well as he had ordered; she seemed eager to do better. Nothing seemed to make her more furious than to see me with a newspaper. She seemed to think the danger lay there. She has rushed at me with a face made up entirely of rage and snatched a newspaper from me in a way that fully revealed her fear. She was a quick-minded woman; and a little experience soon proved to her satisfaction that education and slavery could not exist together.

From this time on I was watched very closely. If I stayed in a separate room for any length of time, I was sure to be suspected of having a book, and was at once called to account for myself. But all of this came too late. The first step had already been taken. My mistress, in teaching me the alphabet, had given me the _inch,_ and no precaution could stop me from taking the _ell._

The plan I adopted, and the one that worked best for me, was to make friends of all the little white boys I met in the street. As many of these as I could, I turned into teachers. With their kindly help, given at different times and in different places, I finally managed to learn to read. Whenever I was sent on errands, I always took my book with me, and by hurrying through one part of an errand, I found time to get a lesson before I returned. I also used to carry bread with me—there was always plenty of it in the house, and I was always welcome to it; for in this respect I was much better off than many of the poor white children in our neighborhood. This bread I gave away to the hungry little urchins, who in return would give me that far more valuable bread of knowledge. I am strongly tempted to give the names of two or three of those little boys, as a testimony to the gratitude and affection I feel for them; but prudence forbids it—not that it would harm me, but it might get them into trouble; for it is almost an unpardonable offense to teach slaves to read in this Christian country. It is enough to say of the dear little fellows that they lived on Philpot Street, very near Durgin and Bailey’s ship-yard. I used to talk this matter of slavery over with them. I would sometimes tell them I wished I could be as free as they would be when they grew to be men. “You will be free as soon as you are twenty-one, _but I am a slave for life!_ Have I not as good a right to be free as you do?” These words used to trouble them; they would show me the keenest sympathy and console me with the hope that something would happen by which I might become free.

I was now about twelve years old, and the thought of being _a slave for life_ began to weigh heavily on my heart. Right about this time, I got hold of a book called “The Columbian Orator.” Every chance I got, I read this book. Among much other interesting material, I found in it a dialogue between a master and his slave. The slave was portrayed as having run away from his master three times. The dialogue presented the conversation that took place between them when the slave was captured for the third time. In it, the master laid out the whole argument in favor of slavery, all of which the slave then dismantled. The slave was made to say some very clever and impressive things in reply to his master—things that had the intended though unexpected effect; for the conversation ended in the master’s voluntary freeing of the slave.

In the same book, I came upon one of Sheridan’s mighty speeches on behalf of Catholic emancipation. These were precious documents to me. I read them over and over again with undiminished interest. They gave voice to interesting thoughts of my own soul, which had often flashed through my mind only to fade away for lack of expression. The lesson I drew from the dialogue was the power of truth over the conscience of even a slaveholder. What I got from Sheridan was a bold denunciation of slavery and a powerful defense of human rights. Reading these documents enabled me to put my thoughts into words and to answer the arguments brought forward to support slavery; but while they relieved me of one difficulty, they brought on another even more painful than the one they had relieved. The more I read, the more I came to abhor and detest my enslavers. I could see them in no other light than as a band of successful robbers who had left their homes, gone to Africa, stolen us from our homes, and reduced us to slavery in a strange land. I loathed them as the meanest and most wicked of men. As I read and reflected on the subject, behold!—that very discontent which Master Hugh had predicted would follow my learning to read had already arrived, to torment and sting my soul into unspeakable anguish. As I writhed under it, I would at times feel that learning to read had been a curse rather than a blessing. It had shown me my wretched condition without offering any remedy. It had opened my eyes to the horrible pit, but gave me no ladder to climb out of it. In moments of agony, I envied my fellow-slaves their dullness. I have often wished myself a beast. I would have preferred the condition of the lowest reptile to my own. Anything, no matter what, to be rid of thinking! It was this endless thinking about my condition that tormented me. There was no escaping it. It was forced upon me by every object within sight or hearing, living or lifeless. The silver trumpet of freedom had roused my soul to permanent wakefulness. Freedom now appeared, never to vanish again. It was heard in every sound and seen in everything. It was always there to torment me with a sense of my wretched condition. I saw nothing without seeing it, I heard nothing without hearing it, and felt nothing without feeling it. It looked out from every star, it smiled in every calm, breathed in every wind, and moved in every storm.

I often found myself regretting my own existence and wishing myself dead; and were it not for the hope of being free, I have no doubt that I would have killed myself, or done something for which I would have been killed. While in this state of mind, I was eager to hear anyone speak of slavery. I was a ready listener. Every now and then, I would hear something about the abolitionists. It was some time before I discovered what the word meant. It was always used in such contexts as to make it an intriguing word to me. If a slave ran away and managed to get clear, or if a slave killed his master, set fire to a barn, or did anything that struck a slaveholder as very wrong, it was spoken of as the fruit of _abolition._ Hearing the word in this connection so often, I set out to learn what it meant. The dictionary gave me little or no help. I found that it meant “the act of abolishing;” but then I did not know what was to be abolished. Here I was baffled. I did not dare ask anyone about its meaning, for I was sure it was something they wanted me to know very little about. After waiting patiently, I got hold of one of our city papers, which contained a report of the number of petitions from the north praying for the abolition of slavery in the District of Columbia and of the slave trade between the States. From this time on I understood the words _abolition_ and _abolitionist,_ and I always drew near whenever that word was spoken, expecting to hear something of importance to myself and my fellow-slaves. The light broke in on me little by little. One day I went down to the wharf of Mr. Waters; and seeing two Irishmen unloading a scow of stone, I went over, unasked, and helped them. When we had finished, one of them came up to me and asked if I were a slave. I told him I was. He asked, “Are ye a slave for life?” I told him that I was. The good Irishman seemed deeply moved by my answer. He said to the other that it was a pity so fine a little fellow as myself should be a slave for life. He said it was a shame to hold me. They both advised me to run away to the north; there I would find friends, and there I would be free. I pretended not to be interested in what they said, and acted as if I did not understand them; for I feared they might be treacherous. White men have been known to encourage slaves to escape, and then, to claim the reward, catch them and return them to their masters. I was afraid these seemingly good men might do the same to me; but all the same I remembered their advice, and from that time on I resolved to run away. I looked forward to a time when it would be safe for me to escape. I was too young to think of doing it immediately; besides, I wanted to learn how to write, since I might have need to write my own pass. I comforted myself with the hope that one day I would find a good chance. In the meantime, I would learn to write.

The idea of how I might learn to write came to me from being in Durgin and Bailey’s ship-yard, where I often saw the ship carpenters, after hewing a piece of timber and getting it ready for use, write on it the name of the part of the ship it was meant for. When a piece of timber was meant for the larboard side, it would be marked like this—“L.” When a piece was for the starboard side, it would be marked like this—“S.” A piece for the larboard side forward would be marked like this—“L. F.” When a piece was for the starboard side forward, it would be marked like this—“S. F.” For larboard aft, it would be marked like this—“L. A.” For starboard aft, it would be marked like this—“S. A.” I soon learned the names of these letters and what they stood for when placed on a piece of timber in the ship-yard. I immediately began copying them, and in a short time I was able to make the four letters named. After that, whenever I met a boy I knew could write, I would tell him I could write as well as he could. His next words would be, “I don’t believe you. Let me see you try it.” I would then make the letters I had been lucky enough to learn, and ask him to beat that. In this way I got a good many lessons in writing, which I quite possibly would never have gotten in any other way. During this time, my copy-book was the board fence, the brick wall, and the pavement; my pen and ink was a lump of chalk. With these, I learned mostly how to write. I then began copying the italics in Webster’s Spelling Book, and kept at it until I could make them all without looking at the book. By this time, my little Master Thomas had gone to school, learned how to write, and filled up a number of copy-books. These had been brought home, shown to some of our near neighbors, and then set aside. My mistress used to go to class meeting at the Wilk Street meetinghouse every Monday afternoon and leave me to look after the house. When left like this, I would spend the time writing in the spaces left in Master Thomas’s copy-book, copying what he had written. I kept doing this until I could write a hand very much like Master Thomas’s. And so, after a long, tedious effort over many years, I finally succeeded in learning how to write.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Very soon after I went to live in Baltimore, my old master’s youngest son, Richard, died; and about three years and six months after his death, my old master, Captain Anthony, died as well. He left only his son, Andrew, and his daughter, Lucretia, to share his estate. He died while visiting his daughter at Hillsborough. Cut off so unexpectedly, he left no will directing how his property should be disposed of. It therefore became necessary to have the property appraised, so that it could be divided equally between Mrs. Lucretia and Master Andrew. I was sent for at once, to be valued along with the rest of the property. Once again my whole being rose up in loathing of slavery. I now understood my degraded condition in a new way. Before this, I had grown, if not numb to my situation, at least partly so. I left Baltimore with a young heart weighed down by sadness and a soul full of dread. I took passage with Captain Rowe, in the schooner Wild Cat, and after a sail of about twenty-four hours I found myself near the place where I was born. I had now been away from it for nearly, if not quite, five years. Even so, I remembered the place very well. I had been only about five years old when I left it to go and live with my old master on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation, so that I was now between ten and eleven years old.

We were all ranked together at the appraisal. Men and women, old and young, married and single, were ranked alongside horses, sheep, and swine. There were horses and men, cattle and women, pigs and children, all assigned the same rank on the scale of being, and all subjected to the same crude examination. Silver-haired age and lively youth, young women and married women, all had to submit to the same indecent inspection. In that moment, I saw more clearly than ever the brutalizing effect of slavery on both the slave and the slaveholder.

After the appraisal came the division. I have no words to express the intense excitement and deep anxiety we poor slaves felt during this time. Our fate for the rest of our lives was about to be decided. We had no more say in that decision than the animals among whom we had been ranked. A single word from the white men was enough—against all our wishes, prayers, and pleadings—to tear apart forever the dearest friends, the dearest kindred, and the strongest bonds known to human beings. On top of the pain of separation, there was the dreadful fear of falling into the hands of Master Andrew. We all knew him to be a most cruel wretch—a habitual drunkard who, through his reckless mismanagement and shameless dissipation, had already squandered a large part of his father’s property. We all felt we might as well be sold outright to the Georgia traders as pass into his hands, for we knew that this would inevitably be our fate—a fate we all regarded with the utmost horror and dread.

I suffered more anxiety than most of my fellow slaves. I had known what it was to be treated kindly; they had known nothing of the sort. They had seen little or nothing of the world. They were truly men and women of sorrow, well acquainted with grief. Their backs had grown familiar with the bloody lash, until they had become hardened to it; mine was still tender, for while in Baltimore I had received few whippings, and few slaves could claim a kinder master and mistress than I had. The thought of passing out of their hands into those of Master Andrew—a man who, only a few days before, had given me a sample of his bloody temper by seizing my little brother by the throat, throwing him to the ground, and stamping on his head with the heel of his boot until the blood gushed from his nose and ears—was well suited to make me anxious about what lay ahead. After committing this savage outrage upon my brother, he turned to me and said that was exactly how he intended to treat me one of these days—meaning, I suppose, once I came into his possession.

Thanks to a kind Providence, I fell to Mrs. Lucretia’s share, and was sent straight back to Baltimore to live once again in the family of Master Hugh. Their joy at my return matched their sorrow at my departure. It was a happy day for me. I had escaped something worse than a lion’s jaws. I had been away from Baltimore, for the appraisal and division, just about one month, yet it had felt like six.

Very soon after my return to Baltimore, my mistress, Lucretia, died, leaving behind her husband and one child, Amanda; and a very short time after her death, Master Andrew died as well. Now all the property of my old master, slaves included, was in the hands of strangers—strangers who had had nothing to do with building it up. Not a single slave was set free. All remained slaves, from the youngest to the oldest. If any one thing in my experience, more than any other, served to deepen my conviction of the hellish character of slavery, and to fill me with unspeakable loathing of slaveholders, it was their base ingratitude toward my poor old grandmother. She had served my old master faithfully from her youth into old age. She had been the source of all his wealth; she had peopled his plantation with slaves; she had become a great-grandmother in his service. She had rocked him in infancy, attended him in childhood, served him throughout his life, and at his death wiped the cold death-sweat from his icy brow and closed his eyes forever. Yet she was still left a slave—a slave for life—a slave in the hands of strangers; and in their hands she watched her children, her grandchildren, and her great-grandchildren divided up, like so many sheep, without being granted even the small privilege of a single word about their fate or her own. And to crown their base ingratitude and fiendish cruelty, my grandmother, who was now very old, having outlived my old master and all his children, having seen the beginning and the end of every one of them—when her present owners found that she was of little value, her frame already racked with the pains of old age and complete helplessness rapidly overtaking her once active limbs, they carried her off to the woods, built her a little hut, put up a small mud chimney, and then graciously left her to support herself there in utter loneliness; thus, in effect, turning her out to die! If my poor old grandmother is still alive, she lives to suffer in total loneliness; she lives to remember and mourn the loss of her children, the loss of her grandchildren, and the loss of her great-grandchildren. They are, in the words of the slave’s poet, Whittier,—

“Gone, gone, sold and gone To the rice swamp dank and lone, Where the slave-whip ceaseless swings, Where the noisome insect stings, Where the fever-demon strews Poison with the falling dews, Where the sickly sunbeams glare Through the hot and misty air:— Gone, gone, sold and gone To the rice swamp dank and lone, From Virginia hills and waters— Woe is me, my stolen daughters!”

The hearth is desolate. The children—the innocent children—who once sang and danced in her presence are gone. She gropes her way, in the darkness of old age, for a drink of water. Instead of the voices of her children, she hears by day the moaning of the dove, and by night the screeching of the hideous owl. All is gloom. The grave is at the door. And now, when she is weighed down by the aches and pains of old age, when her head bends toward her feet, when the beginning and the ending of human life meet, and helpless infancy and painful old age come together—at this time, this time of greatest need, the time for that tenderness and affection which only children can show toward a declining parent—my poor old grandmother, the devoted mother of twelve children, is left all alone, in that little hut, before a few dim embers. She stands—she sits—she staggers—she falls—she groans—she dies—and not one of her children or grandchildren is present to wipe the cold sweat of death from her wrinkled brow, or to lay her fallen remains beneath the sod. Will a righteous God not call them to account for these things?

About two years after the death of Mrs. Lucretia, Master Thomas married his second wife. Her name was Rowena Hamilton. She was the eldest daughter of Mr. William Hamilton. Master now lived in St. Michael’s. Not long after his marriage, a falling-out arose between him and Master Hugh; and as a way of punishing his brother, he took me away from him to live with himself at St. Michael’s. Here I went through another deeply painful separation. It was not, however, as severe as the one I had dreaded at the division of the property; for in the meantime a great change had come over Master Hugh and his once kind and affectionate wife. The effect of brandy on him, and of slavery on her, had brought about a disastrous change in the character of both, so that, as far as they were concerned, I felt I had little to lose by the move. But it was not to them that I was attached. It was to those little Baltimore boys that I felt the strongest attachment. I had received many good lessons from them, and was still receiving them, and the thought of leaving them was painful indeed. I was leaving, too, with no hope of ever being allowed to return. Master Thomas had said he would never let me come back. The rift between himself and his brother he considered impossible to cross.
I then had reason to regret that I had not at least made the attempt to carry out my resolve to run away; for the chances of success are ten times greater from the city than from the country.

I sailed from Baltimore for St. Michael’s in the sloop Amanda, Captain Edward Dodson. During the voyage, I paid close attention to the route the steamboats took on their way to Philadelphia. I found that, instead of heading down the bay, once they reached North Point they went up it, in a north-easterly direction. I considered this knowledge to be of the utmost importance. My determination to run away was revived once more. I resolved to wait only until a favorable opportunity presented itself. When that came, I was determined to be gone.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: I have now reached a period of my life when I can give exact dates. I left Baltimore and went to live with Master Thomas Auld at St. Michael’s in March, 1832. By then it had been more than seven years since I had lived with him in the household of my old master, on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation. As a result, we were now nearly complete strangers to each other. He was a new master to me, and I was a new slave to him. I knew nothing of his temper or disposition, and he knew just as little of mine. A very short time, however, brought us into full knowledge of each other. I came to know his wife just as well as I came to know him. They were well matched, for they were equally mean and cruel. Now, for the first time in more than seven years, I was made to feel the painful gnawing of hunger—something I had not experienced since leaving Colonel Lloyd’s plantation. It had been hard enough back then, when I could look back on no period in which I had ever had enough to eat. It was ten times harder now, after living in Master Hugh’s family, where I had always had plenty of food, and good food at that. I have said that Master Thomas was a mean man. He was. Among slaveholders, failing to give a slave enough to eat is regarded as the most extreme form of meanness. The rule is that, no matter how coarse the food may be, there should at least be enough of it. That is the theory, and in the part of Maryland I came from, it is the general practice—though there are many exceptions. Master Thomas gave us enough of neither coarse food nor fine. There were four of us slaves in the kitchen—my sister Eliza, my aunt Priscilla, Henny, and myself—and we were allowed less than half a bushel of corn-meal per week, and very little else, whether meat or vegetables. It was not enough for us to live on. We were therefore reduced to the wretched necessity of surviving at our neighbors’ expense. We did this by begging and stealing, whichever was easier in our time of need, the one being considered just as legitimate as the other. Many times we poor creatures were nearly perishing with hunger while food lay in abundance, rotting in the safe and the smoke-house, and our pious mistress knew it; and yet that mistress and her husband would kneel every morning and pray that God would bless them in basket and store!

As bad as all slaveholders are, we rarely meet one who lacks every element of character that commands respect. My master was one of this rare sort. I do not know of a single noble act he ever performed. The leading trait in his character was meanness, and if there was any other quality in his nature, it was made to serve this one. He was mean, and, like most other mean men, he lacked the ability to hide his meanness. Captain Auld was not born a slaveholder. He had been a poor man, master only of a Bay craft. He came into possession of all his slaves through marriage; and of all men, those who take up slaveholding by adoption are the worst. He was cruel, but cowardly. He gave commands without firmness. In enforcing his rules he was sometimes rigid and sometimes lax. At times he spoke to his slaves with the firmness of Napoleon and the fury of a demon; at other times he might easily have been mistaken for a lost traveler asking directions. He did nothing on his own. He might have passed for a lion, were it not for his ears. In every noble thing he attempted, his own meanness showed through most plainly. His airs, his words, and his actions were the airs, words, and actions of born slaveholders, and, being merely put on, they were awkward enough. He was not even a good imitator. He had every inclination to deceive but not the power.
