Having no resources within himself, he was forced to copy many others, and being a mere copyist, he was forever the victim of inconsistency; and as a result, he was an object of contempt, even in the eyes of his own slaves. The luxury of having slaves of his own to wait on him was something new to him and something he was unprepared for. He was a slaveholder without the ability to hold slaves. He found himself incapable of managing his slaves by force, by fear, or by fraud. We seldom called him “master;” we generally called him “Captain Auld,” and were hardly inclined to give him any title at all. I have no doubt that our conduct had a great deal to do with making him seem awkward, and therefore irritable. Our lack of reverence for him must have puzzled him greatly. He wanted us to call him master but lacked the firmness needed to command us to do so. His wife used to insist that we call him so, but to no effect. In August, 1832, my master attended a Methodist camp-meeting held in the Bay-side, Talbot county, and there he experienced religion. I held a faint hope that his conversion would lead him to free his slaves, and that, if it did not do that, it would at least make him kinder and more humane. I was disappointed on both counts. It neither made him humane toward his slaves nor moved him to free them. If it had any effect on his character, it made him more cruel and hateful in everything he did; for I believe he was a far worse man after his conversion than before. Before his conversion, he relied on his own depravity to shield and sustain him in his savage barbarity; but after his conversion, he found religious sanction and support for his slaveholding cruelty. He made the loudest claims to piety. His house was a house of prayer. He prayed morning, noon, and night. He very soon distinguished himself among his brethren and was quickly made a class-leader and exhorter. He was very active in revivals, and he proved himself a useful instrument in the church’s hands for converting many souls. His house was a home for the preachers. They used to take great pleasure in coming there to stay; for while he starved us, he stuffed them. We have had three or four preachers there at once. The names of those who came most often while I lived there were Mr. Storks, Mr. Ewery, Mr. Humphry, and Mr. Hickey. I have also seen Mr. George Cookman at our house. We slaves loved Mr. Cookman. We believed him to be a good man. We thought he had been instrumental in getting Mr. Samuel Harrison, a very rich slaveholder, to free his slaves; and somehow we got the impression that he was working to bring about the emancipation of all slaves. Whenever he was at our house, we were sure to be called in to prayers. When the others were there, we were sometimes called in and sometimes not. Mr. Cookman took more notice of us than any of the other ministers. He could not be among us without showing his sympathy for us, and, ignorant as we were, we had the sense to see it.

While I lived with my master in St. Michael’s, there was a young white man, a Mr. Wilson, who proposed to hold a Sabbath school to teach those slaves who might wish to learn to read the New Testament. We met only three times, when Mr. West and Mr. Fairbanks, both class-leaders, along with many others, descended on us with sticks and other missiles, drove us off, and forbade us to meet again. So ended our little Sabbath school in the pious town of St. Michael’s.

I have said that my master found religious sanction for his cruelty. As one example among many that prove this charge, I will give an account of a single fact. I have seen him tie up a lame young woman and whip her with a heavy cowskin across her naked shoulders, drawing the warm red blood until it dripped; and, to justify the bloody deed, he would quote this passage of Scripture—“He that knoweth his master’s will, and doeth it not, shall be beaten with many stripes.”

Master would keep this lacerated young woman tied up in that horrible position for four or five hours at a time. I have known him to tie her up early in the morning and whip her before breakfast; then leave her, go to his store, return at dinner, and whip her again, cutting into the places already raw from his cruel lash. The secret behind master’s cruelty toward “Henny” lies in the fact that she was almost helpless. When she was quite a child, she fell into the fire and burned herself horribly. Her hands were so badly burned that she never regained the use of them. She could do very little except carry heavy loads. To master she was nothing but an expense; and since he was a mean man, she was a constant offense to him. He seemed eager to get the poor girl out of existence. He gave her away once to his sister; but, being a poor gift, his sister was not inclined to keep her. Finally, my benevolent master, to use his own words, “set her adrift to take care of herself.” Here was a recently converted man, holding on to the mother while at the same time turning out her helpless child to starve and die! Master Thomas was one of the many pious slaveholders who hold slaves for the very charitable purpose of taking care of them.

My master and I had quite a number of disagreements. He found me unsuited to his purposes. My life in the city, he said, had had a very harmful effect on me. It had nearly ruined me for every good purpose and prepared me for everything that was bad. One of my greatest faults was letting his horse run away and go down to his father-in-law’s farm, which was about five miles from St. Michael’s. I would then have to go after it. My reason for this kind of carelessness—or carefulness—was that I could always get something to eat when I went there. Master William Hamilton, my master’s father-in-law, always gave his slaves enough to eat. I never left there hungry, no matter how urgent the need for me to hurry back. At last Master Thomas said he would put up with it no longer. I had lived with him nine months, during which he had given me a number of severe whippings, all to no good purpose. He decided to put me out, as he said, to be broken; and for this purpose he hired me out for one year to a man named Edward Covey. Mr. Covey was a poor man, a farm-renter. He rented the place he lived on, as well as the hands he used to work it. Mr. Covey had earned a very high reputation for breaking young slaves, and this reputation was of immense value to him. It allowed him to get his farm worked at far less expense to himself than he could have managed without it. Some slaveholders thought it not much of a loss to let Mr. Covey have their slaves for a year, for the sake of the training they underwent, without any other payment. Because of this reputation, he could hire young help with great ease. On top of Mr. Covey’s natural good qualities, he was a professor of religion—a pious soul—a member and class-leader in the Methodist church. All of this added weight to his reputation as a “nigger-breaker.” I knew all of these facts, having been told them by a young man who had lived there. Even so, I made the change gladly; for I was sure of getting enough to eat, which is no small consideration to a hungry man.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: On January 1, 1833, I left Master Thomas's house and moved in with Mr. Covey. For the first time in my life I was a field hand, and at the work I felt clumsier than a country boy turned loose in a big city. I had been there only a week when Mr. Covey gave me a brutal whipping — slicing open my back, drawing blood, raising welts on my skin as thick as my little finger. Here is how it came about. Very early on one of the coldest mornings that January, he sent me into the woods to haul back a load of wood, and handed me a team of oxen that had never been broken. He pointed out which was the in-hand ox and which the off-hand one, looped the end of a heavy rope around the horns of the in-hand ox, gave me the loose end, and warned me to hang on tight if the animals bolted. I had never driven oxen in my life, so naturally I was hopeless at it. Still, I managed to reach the edge of the woods without much trouble. But I had only gone a few rods in when the oxen panicked and tore off at full speed, slamming the cart into trees and over stumps in the most terrifying way. At every moment I braced for my skull to be smashed against a tree. After charging on like this for a good distance, they finally flipped the cart, ramming it hard into a tree, and flung themselves into a thick patch of brush. How I came out alive I cannot say. There I stood, completely alone, deep in a strange wood, my cart overturned and wrecked, my oxen tangled in the saplings, and nobody to help me. After a long, hard struggle I got the cart upright again, the oxen freed, and the team re-yoked. I drove on to the spot where I had been chopping the day before, and loaded the cart down heavily, figuring a heavy load might calm the oxen. Then I started for home. By now half the day was gone. I made it out of the woods safely and felt I was past the worst. I stopped the team to open the gate, and right then, before I could grab the ox-rope, the oxen bolted again — they crashed through the gate, caught it between the wheel and the body of the cart, ripped it to pieces, and came within inches of crushing me against the gatepost. So twice in one short day I escaped death by sheer luck. When I got back I told Mr. Covey everything that had happened and how. He ordered me straight back into the woods, and came after me himself. The moment I reached the woods he caught up, told me to halt the cart, and said he would teach me to waste my time and smash gates. He walked over to a big gum-tree, cut three large switches with his axe, trimmed them neatly with his pocketknife, and ordered me to take off my clothes. I gave him no answer and stood there still dressed. He gave the order again. Again I said nothing and made no move to strip. At that he lunged at me like a tiger, tore the clothes off me, and lashed me until the switches were worn out, cutting so savagely that the marks stayed visible long after. This whipping was only the first of many just like it, all for similar offenses.

I lived with Mr. Covey for a year. For the first six months of it, hardly a week went by without a whipping, and my back was rarely free of sores. Almost any clumsiness on my part was excuse enough for the lash. We were worked right up to the limit of what a body could bear. We were up long before dawn, the horses fed, and at the first hint of daylight we were off to the field with our hoes and plough-teams. He gave us plenty to eat but barely a moment to eat it — often we had less than five minutes for a meal. We were frequently in the field from first light until the last fading ray was gone, and when the fodder had to be saved, midnight often found us still out there binding blades.

Covey was right out there with us. Here is how he kept it up: he spent most of his afternoons in bed, then came out fresh in the evening to drive us on with his words, his example, and often his whip. He was one of the rare slaveholders who actually worked with his own hands, and he was a hard worker. Because he did the labor himself, he knew exactly how much a man or a boy could manage, and you could never fool him. The work went on nearly as well when he was away as when he was present, because he had a knack for making us feel he was always watching. He pulled this off by catching us off guard. He almost never came up to where we were working in plain sight if he could do it in secret — surprise was always his aim. He was so sly that among ourselves we called him "the snake." When we were working the cornfield, he would sometimes crawl on his hands and knees to keep from being seen, then suddenly rise up almost on top of us and yell, "Ha, ha! Come, come! Dash on, dash on!" Since this was his method of attack, it was never safe to pause for a single minute. He came on us like a thief in the night. To us he seemed forever close at hand — under every tree, behind every stump, in every bush, at every window on the place. Sometimes he would mount his horse as if he were headed for St. Michael's, seven miles off, and half an hour later you would spot him crouched in a corner of the wood-fence, tracking every move the slaves made. For this he would leave his horse tied up in the woods. Other times he would walk over and give us orders as if he were about to set out on a long trip, turn his back, and act like he was going up to the house to get ready — but before he had gone halfway there he would wheel around and crawl into a fence-corner or behind some tree, and watch us until sundown.

Mr. Covey's real talent was for deception. His whole life was given over to planning and pulling off the crudest lies. Whatever learning or religion he had, he bent to fit his urge to deceive. He seemed to believe he could even deceive God Almighty. He would say a short prayer in the morning and a long one at night, and, strange as it sounds, few men could at times look more devout than he did. The family worship always opened with singing, and since he was a wretched singer himself, the job of starting the hymn usually fell to me. He would read out the hymn and nod for me to begin. Sometimes I would; other times I would not. My refusal almost always threw everything into confusion. To show he did not need me, he would launch in and lurch through the hymn in the most off-key way imaginable. In that frame of mind he prayed with even more than his usual fervor. Poor man — such was his nature, and his skill at deceiving, that I honestly believe he sometimes fooled himself into the solemn conviction that he was a sincere worshipper of the Most High God; and this at a time when he could be said to be forcing his woman slave into the sin of adultery. Here are the facts. Mr. Covey was a poor man just starting out in life, able to afford only one slave, and — shocking as it is — he bought her, by his own account, as a breeder. The woman's name was Caroline. He bought her from Mr. Thomas Lowe, who lived about six miles from St. Michael's. She was large and strong, around twenty years old, and had already borne one child, which proved her to be exactly what he was after. After buying her, he hired a married man from Mr. Samuel Harrison to live with him for a year, and every night he locked the man up with her. The result was that at the end of the year the poor woman gave birth to twins. This outcome seemed to delight Mr. Covey, both with the man and with the wretched woman. So great was the joy of him and his wife that nothing they could do for Caroline during her confinement was too good or too much trouble. The children were counted as a fine addition to his wealth.

If there was ever a stretch of my life when I was forced to swallow slavery at its most bitter, it was those first six months with Mr. Covey. We worked in every kind of weather. It was never too hot or too cold; no rain, wind, hail, or snow ever came down hard enough to keep us out of the field. Work, work, work was hardly more the rule by day than by night. The longest days were too short for him, and the shortest nights too long. I was somewhat hard to handle when I first arrived, but a few months of that treatment tamed me. Mr. Covey managed to break me — broken in body, soul, and spirit. My natural springiness was crushed, my mind went dull, the desire to read drained away, the bright spark that once lived in my eye went out, the dark night of slavery shut down over me, and there you had a man turned into a brute.

Sunday was my only time off, and I passed it in a kind of animal stupor, drifting between sleep and waking under some big tree. Now and then I would sit up, and a flash of restless longing for freedom would shoot through me, with a faint glimmer of hope that flickered a moment and then died. I would sink back down, grieving over how miserable I was. At times I was tempted to take my own life, and Covey's too, but a mix of hope and fear always held me back. My suffering on that plantation feels now more like a dream than a hard fact.

Our house stood only a few rods from the Chesapeake Bay, whose wide surface was forever white with sails from every corner of the inhabited world. Those lovely ships, dressed in the purest white — a delight to the eyes of free men — were to me so many ghosts wrapped in burial cloth, there to terrify me and torment me with thoughts of my wretched state. Often, in the deep hush of a summer Sabbath, I stood entirely alone on the high banks of that great bay and followed, with a heavy heart and tears in my eyes, the endless line of sails gliding off toward the open ocean. The sight always struck me with tremendous force. My thoughts had to find a voice, and there, with no listener but God, I would pour out the grief of my soul in my own crude way, calling out to that drifting crowd of ships:—

"You have slipped your moorings and you are free; I am held fast in my chains, a slave. You glide along happily before the soft breeze, while I drag along miserably before the bloody whip. You are freedom's swift-winged angels, circling the whole world, while I am locked in bands of iron. Oh, if only I were free! Oh, to stand on one of your proud decks, under the shelter of your wings! But no — between you and me the muddy waters keep rolling on. Sail on, sail on. Oh, that I could go too! If only I could swim! If only I could fly! Oh, why was I born a man, only to be made into a brute? The happy ship is gone now, vanishing into the dim distance, and I am left behind in the deepest hell of slavery without end. O God, save me! God, set me free! Let me be free! Is there even a God? Why am I a slave? I will run away — I will not stand it. Caught or clear, I'll try it. I might as well die of the chills as of the fever; I have only one life to lose. I might as well be killed running as die where I stand. Just think of it — a hundred miles straight north, and I am free! Try it? Yes! With God's help, I will. It cannot be that I am meant to live and die a slave. I will take to the water. This very bay will one day carry me into freedom. The steamboats run a northeast course out of North Point — I'll do the same, and when I reach the head of the bay I'll set my canoe loose and walk straight through Delaware into Pennsylvania. Once I'm there, I won't need a pass; I can travel without being stopped. Let the first chance only come, and, whatever happens, I'm gone. Until then I'll try to hold up under the yoke. I'm not the only slave in the world — why should I fret? I can stand as much as any of them. Besides, I'm only a boy, and every boy is bound to someone. Maybe all this misery in slavery will only sharpen my happiness once I'm free. A better day is coming."
That is how I used to think, and that is how I used to talk to myself — driven nearly to madness one moment, and the next making my peace with my miserable lot.

I have already hinted that my situation was far worse during the first six months at Mr. Covey's than in the last six. What brought about the change in how he treated me marks a turning point in my humble story. You have seen how a man was made a slave; now you will see how a slave was made a man. On one of the hottest days of August 1833, Bill Smith, William Hughes, a slave named Eli, and I were busy fanning wheat. Hughes was clearing away the fanned wheat from the front of the fan, Eli was turning, Smith was feeding, and I was carrying the wheat over to the fan. The work was simple, calling for muscle rather than brains, but to someone wholly unused to it, it was punishing. Around three o'clock that afternoon I gave out — my strength failed, my head began pounding violently, I was swept with terrible dizziness, and every limb shook. Feeling it coming on, I braced myself, sure that stopping was out of the question. I held out as long as I could still stagger to the hopper with the grain. When I could no longer stay on my feet, I dropped, feeling as though some enormous weight were pinning me down. The fan of course came to a halt, since everyone had his own task and no one could do another man's work and keep his own going at the same time.

Mr. Covey was at the house, about a hundred yards from the treading-yard where we were fanning. The moment he heard the fan stop, he came straight over to where we were and hurriedly demanded to know what was wrong. Bill told him I was sick and there was no one left to bring wheat to the fan. By then I had crawled off under the post-and-rail fence that enclosed the yard, hoping to ease my misery by getting out of the sun. He asked where I was, and one of the hands told him. He came to the spot, looked at me a while, and asked what the matter was. I answered as best I could, for I barely had the strength to speak. At that he kicked me savagely in the side and ordered me to get up. I tried, but fell back. He kicked me again and told me again to rise. I tried once more and managed to get to my feet — but as I bent to grab the tub I had been feeding the fan with, I staggered and went down again. While I lay there, Mr. Covey picked up the hickory slat Hughes had been using to strike off the half-bushel measure and brought it down hard on my head, opening a large gash that bled freely; and with that he again told me to get up. I made no move to obey, having now made up my mind to let him do his worst. A short while after that blow, my head began to clear, and Mr. Covey had by then left me to my own devices. At that moment I decided, for the first time, to go to my master, lodge a complaint, and ask for his protection. To do it I would have to walk seven miles that afternoon, which under the circumstances was a brutal undertaking. I was terribly weak — as much from the kicks and blows as from the fierce attack of sickness I had been through. Still, I watched my chance, and while Covey was looking the other way, I set out for St. Michael's. I had gotten a fair distance on my way toward the woods when Covey spotted me and shouted for me to come back, threatening what he would do if I refused. I ignored both his calls and his threats and pushed on toward the woods as fast as my feeble state allowed; and thinking he might overtake me if I stayed on the road, I went through the woods, keeping far enough from the road to avoid being seen but close enough not to lose my way. I had not gone far before my little strength failed me again. I could go no farther. I fell down and lay there a long while, the blood still seeping from the wound on my head. For a time I thought I would bleed to death, and I believe I would have, had the blood not matted my hair enough to close the wound. After lying there about three-quarters of an hour, I steadied myself again and started on, through bogs and briars, barefoot and bareheaded, tearing my feet at nearly every step; and after a journey of about seven miles that took some five hours to make, I reached my master's store. The state I was in would have moved anyone but a heart of iron. From the top of my head to my feet I was covered in blood — my hair clotted with dust and blood, my shirt stiff with it. I must have looked like a man who had broken out of a den of wild beasts and barely gotten away. Looking like that, I stood before my master and humbly begged him to step in with his authority and protect me. I told him the whole story as well as I could, and as I spoke it seemed at times to move him. He would pace the floor and try to excuse Covey by saying he supposed I must have deserved it. He asked what I wanted. I told him I wanted a new home, because as sure as I lived with Mr. Covey again I would only live with him to die with him; Covey would surely kill me, and was well on the way to it. Master Thomas laughed off the notion that Covey was any danger to my life, said he knew the man, that he was a good man, and that he could not think of taking me away from him — that if he did, he would lose the whole year's wages, that I belonged to Covey for a year and had to go back to him no matter what, and that I had better not bother him with any more such stories, or he would get hold of me himself. After threatening me like that, he gave me a huge dose of salts, told me I could stay in St. Michael's that night, since it was already quite late, but that I had to be off back to Mr. Covey's first thing in the morning — and that if I wasn't, he would get hold of me, which meant he would whip me. I stayed the night, and as ordered I set out for Covey's in the morning, Saturday morning, worn out in body and broken in spirit. I had no supper that night and no breakfast that morning. I reached Covey's around nine o'clock; and just as I was climbing over the fence that separated Mrs. Kemp's fields from ours, out ran Covey with his cowskin to give me another whipping. Before he could get to me, I made it into the cornfield, and since the corn was very high it gave me a place to hide. He looked furious and searched for me a long time. My behavior must have seemed completely senseless to him. Finally he gave up the hunt, figuring, I suppose, that I would have to come home eventually for something to eat, and he would waste no more effort looking. I spent most of that day in the woods, with only two choices before me — go home and be whipped to death, or stay in the woods and starve. That night I ran into Sandy Jenkins, a slave I knew a little. Sandy had a free wife who lived about four miles from Mr. Covey's, and since it was Saturday he was on his way to see her. I told him my situation, and he kindly invited me to go home with him. I went, and we talked the whole matter over while I asked his advice on what I should do. I found Sandy an old hand at giving counsel. He told me very solemnly that I had to go back to Covey, but that before I did, I should go with him to another part of the woods where there was a certain root which, if I carried a piece of it always on my right side, would make it impossible for Mr. Covey, or any other white man, to whip me. He said he had carried it for years, and ever since he had, he had never taken a blow and never expected to as long as he kept it. At first I dismissed the idea that simply carrying a root in my pocket could do any such thing, and I was reluctant to take it; but Sandy pressed the matter earnestly, telling me it could do no harm even if it did no good. To please him I finally took the root and carried it on my right side as he had directed. This was Sunday morning. I started straight for home, and as I came into the yard gate, out came Mr. Covey, on his way to meeting. He spoke to me very kindly, told me to drive the pigs out of a nearby lot, and went on toward church. Now, this strange behavior of Mr. Covey's really did start me wondering whether there was something to the root Sandy had given me; and had it been any day but Sunday, I could have put his manner down to nothing but the power of that root. As it was, I was half ready to believe the root was more than I had first taken it for. All went well until Monday morning, when the root's power was truly put to the test. Long before daylight I was called to go and rub down, curry, and feed the horses. I obeyed, and was glad to. But while I was at it, just as I was tossing down some blades from the loft, Mr. Covey came into the stable with a long rope; and just as I was halfway out of the loft, he grabbed my legs and was about to tie me. As soon as I realized what he was up to, I gave a sudden lunge, and as I did, with him still gripping my legs, I came sprawling onto the stable floor. Mr. Covey seemed to think now that he had me and could do as he liked; but at that instant — where the spirit came from I cannot say — I made up my mind to fight, and acting on that resolve I seized Covey hard by the throat and rose up as I did so. He held on to me and I to him. My resistance was so completely unexpected that Covey seemed thrown off balance. He shook like a leaf. That gave me confidence, and I held him in a tight grip, drawing blood wherever my fingertips dug into him. Mr. Covey soon called out to Hughes for help. Hughes came, and while Covey held me he tried to tie my right hand. As he was at it, I watched my chance and gave him a hard kick just under the ribs. The kick truly sickened Hughes, so that he left me in Mr. Covey's hands. It not only weakened Hughes but Covey too. When Covey saw Hughes doubled over in pain, his nerve gave way. He asked if I meant to keep resisting. I told him I did, whatever came of it — that he had used me like a brute for six months, and I was determined to be used that way no longer. At that he tried to drag me toward a stick lying just outside the stable door, meaning to knock me down. But just as he leaned over to grab it, I caught him by the collar with both hands and snatched him suddenly to the ground. By this time Bill had come up. Covey called on him to help. Bill asked what he could do. Covey said, "Take hold of him, take hold of him!" Bill answered that his master had hired him out to work, not to help whip me, and so he left Covey and me to settle the fight ourselves. We went at it for nearly two hours. At last Covey let me go, puffing and blowing furiously, saying that if I had not resisted he would not have whipped me half so hard. The truth was, he had not whipped me at all. I reckoned he came out far the worse in the bargain, for he had drawn no blood from me, while I had drawn his. In all the six months I spent with Mr. Covey afterward, he never laid the weight of a finger on me in anger. Now and then he would say he had no wish to get hold of me again. "No," I thought, "you needn't — because you'll come off worse than you did before."

This fight with Mr. Covey was the turning point in my life as a slave. It rekindled the few dying embers of freedom in me and brought back a sense of my own manhood. It restored the self-confidence I had lost and fired me once more with a determination to be free. The satisfaction that victory gave me made up for whatever might follow, even death itself. Only the man who has himself fought off by force the bloody arm of slavery can grasp the deep contentment I felt. I felt as I had never felt before. It was a glorious resurrection — out of the tomb of slavery and into the heaven of freedom. My long-crushed spirit rose up, cowardice fell away, bold defiance took its place, and I now resolved that, however long I might stay a slave in name, the day was gone forever when I could be a slave in fact. I let it be known plainly that any white man who meant to whip me would have to kill me first.
From that day on I was never again, in any real sense, whipped, though I stayed a slave for four more years. I had several fights, but I was never whipped.

For a long time I puzzled over why Mr. Covey did not simply have the constable haul me off to the whipping-post to be properly flogged for the crime of raising my hand against a white man in my own defense. The one explanation I can come up with does not fully satisfy me, but I will give it for what it is worth. Mr. Covey had a sky-high reputation as a first-rate overseer and negro-breaker, and that reputation mattered a great deal to him. It was on the line; and had he sent me — a boy of about sixteen — to the public whipping-post, his reputation would have been ruined. So, to protect it, he let me go unpunished.

My actual term of service to Mr. Edward Covey ended on Christmas Day, 1833. The days from Christmas to New Year's are given as holidays, so we were not required to do any work beyond feeding and tending the stock. We looked on this time as our own, granted by our masters' good will, and so we used it — or misused it — pretty much as we pleased. Those of us with families some distance away were usually allowed to spend all six days with them. The time, though, was spent in all sorts of ways. The steady, sober, thoughtful, hardworking ones among us would busy themselves making corn-brooms, mats, horse-collars, and baskets; another set would spend the days hunting opossums, hares, and coons. But by far the most went in for sports and amusements — playing ball, wrestling, footraces, fiddling, dancing, and drinking whisky; and this last way of spending the time pleased our masters most of all. A slave who would work through the holidays was thought by our masters to scarcely deserve them, and was regarded as someone who spurned his master's favor. It was held a disgrace not to get drunk at Christmas, and a man was counted lazy indeed who had not laid by, over the course of the year, enough money for whisky to last him through Christmas.

From what I know of how these holidays affect the slave, I believe they are among the slaveholder's most effective tools for keeping down the spirit of revolt. If slaveholders were suddenly to abandon the practice, I have no doubt at all it would touch off an immediate uprising. These holidays act as conductors, or safety-valves, that carry off the rebellious spirit of enslaved humanity. Without them, the slave would be driven to the wildest desperation; and woe to the slaveholder on the day he dares to remove or block the working of those conductors. I warn him that, should that happen, a spirit will rise up among them more to be dreaded than the most terrifying earthquake.

The holidays are part and parcel of the gross fraud, wrong, and cruelty of slavery. They are presented as a custom set up out of the slaveholders' kindness; but I say flatly that they spring from selfishness and are one of the crudest frauds worked upon the trampled slave. Masters do not grant the slaves this time because they would mind the loss of their labor during it, but because they know it would be dangerous to withhold it. You can see this in the fact that slaveholders like their slaves to spend those days in such a way that they are as glad to see them end as to see them begin. Their aim seems to be to sicken their slaves on the very idea of freedom by plunging them into the lowest forms of dissipation. For instance, slaveholders not only like to see a slave drink of his own accord, but will scheme in various ways to get him drunk. One scheme is to lay bets on their slaves over who can drink the most whisky without getting drunk, and in this way they get whole crowds to drink to excess. So when the slave asks for honest freedom, the cunning slaveholder, knowing how ignorant he is, cheats him with a dose of degrading dissipation, slyly labeled liberty. Most of us used to swallow it down, and the result was just what you would expect — many of us came to feel there was little to choose between liberty and slavery. We felt, and rightly enough, that we might almost as well be slaves to a man as to rum. So when the holidays were over, we staggered up out of the filth we had been wallowing in, took a deep breath, and marched off to the field — feeling, on the whole, rather glad to go, back from what our master had tricked us into mistaking for freedom into the arms of slavery again.

I have said that this way of treating slaves is part of the whole system of fraud and cruelty in slavery, and so it is. The same trick used to sicken the slave on freedom by letting him see only its abuse shows up in other things as well. Take a slave who loves molasses and steals some. In many cases his master will go off to town, buy a large quantity, come back, take up his whip, and order the slave to keep eating molasses until the poor fellow is sick at the very mention of it. The same method is sometimes used to keep slaves from asking for more food than their regular ration. A slave runs through his allowance and asks for more. His master flies into a rage at him; but, unwilling to send him off with nothing, gives him far more than he needs and forces him to eat it all within a set time. Then, if he complains that he cannot eat it, he is said to be satisfied neither full nor fasting, and is whipped for being hard to please. I have plenty more such examples of the same principle drawn from my own observation, but I think the ones I have given are enough. The practice is a very common one.

On January 1, 1834, I left Mr. Covey and went to live with Mr. William Freeland, who lived about three miles from St. Michael's. I soon found Mr. Freeland a very different man from Mr. Covey. He was not rich, but he was what would be called an educated southern gentleman. Mr. Covey, as I have shown, was a well-trained negro-breaker and slave-driver. Freeland, slaveholder though he was, seemed to have some regard for honor, some reverence for justice, and some respect for humanity. Covey seemed utterly dead to any such feelings. Mr. Freeland had many of the faults common to slaveholders — he was very hot-tempered and irritable — but in fairness I must say he was remarkably free of the degrading vices Mr. Covey was forever steeped in. Freeland was open and frank, and we always knew where to find him. Covey was a most cunning deceiver, who could be understood only by those sharp enough to see through his carefully laid frauds. Another advantage I gained in my new master was that he made no claim to religion, no profession of it — and that, in my view, was truly a great advantage. I say without the least hesitation that the religion of the south is nothing but a cloak for the most horrid crimes — a justifier of the most appalling barbarity, a sanctifier of the most hateful frauds, and a dark shelter under which the darkest, foulest, grossest, most hellish deeds of slaveholders find their firmest protection. If I were ever dragged back into the chains of slavery, then next to that enslavement itself I would count belonging to a religious master the worst calamity that could fall on me. For of all the slaveholders I have ever met, religious ones are the worst — the meanest and basest, the most cruel and cowardly of the lot. It was my wretched fate not only to belong to a religious slaveholder but to live in a whole community of such religionists. Right near Mr. Freeland lived the Rev. Daniel Weeden, and in the same neighborhood lived the Rev. Rigby Hopkins, both members and ministers in the Reformed Methodist Church. Among others, Mr. Weeden owned a woman slave whose name I have forgotten. For weeks at a time this woman's back was kept literally raw by the lash of that merciless, religious wretch. He used to hire hands. His rule was that whether a slave behaved well or behaved badly, it was a master's duty to whip him now and then to remind him of his master's authority. Such was his theory, and such was his practice.

Mr. Hopkins was even worse than Mr. Weeden. His chief boast was his skill at managing slaves, and the distinctive feature of his rule was whipping slaves before they had even earned it. He always made sure to have one or more of his slaves to whip every Monday morning. He did it to frighten the rest and strike terror into those who got off. His policy was to whip for the smallest offenses in order to head off larger ones. Mr. Hopkins could always come up with some excuse for whipping a slave. It would amaze anyone not used to a slaveholding life to see how easily a slaveholder can find reasons to whip a slave. A mere look, word, or movement — a mistake, an accident, or a simple inability — any of these is grounds to whip a slave at any time. Does a slave look unhappy? Then he has the devil in him, and it must be whipped out. Does he speak too loudly when his master speaks to him? Then he is getting above himself and should be taken down a notch. Does he forget to take off his hat when a white person comes near? Then he lacks respect and should be whipped for it. Does he ever dare to defend his own conduct when he is scolded for it? Then he is guilty of impudence — one of the gravest crimes a slave can commit. Does he ever dare to suggest doing something differently from the way his master has laid out? Then he is plainly presumptuous and getting above himself, and nothing short of a flogging will set him right. Does he, while ploughing, break a plough — or, while hoeing, break a hoe? It is put down to his carelessness, and for it a slave must always be whipped. Mr. Hopkins could always find something of this kind to justify using the lash, and he rarely passed up such chances. There was not a man in the whole county that the slaves who got to choose their own master would not rather live with than this Rev. Mr. Hopkins. And yet there was not a man anywhere around who made louder professions of religion or was more active in revivals — more faithful at class, love-feast, prayer, and preaching meetings, or more devout in his own household, praying earlier, later, louder, and longer — than this same reverend slave-driver, Rigby Hopkins.

But to come back to Mr. Freeland and my time working for him. Like Mr. Covey he gave us enough to eat; but unlike Mr. Covey he also gave us enough time to eat it. He worked us hard, but always between sunrise and sunset. He demanded a good deal of work, but he gave us good tools to do it with. His farm was large, but he hired enough hands to work it, and with ease compared with many of his neighbors. The treatment I got while in his service was heavenly next to what I had suffered at the hands of Mr. Edward Covey.
Mr. Freeland owned only two slaves himself, named Henry Harris and John Harris. The rest of his hands he hired, and these were myself, Sandy Jenkins,[1] and Handy Caldwell.

[1] This is the same man who gave me the roots to keep Mr. Covey from whipping me. He was "a clever soul." We often used to talk about the fight with Covey, and every time we did, he would claim my success was thanks to the roots he had given me. This kind of superstition is very common among the more ignorant slaves. A slave seldom dies without his death being blamed on some piece of trickery.

Henry and John were quite intelligent, and very soon after I came I managed to stir up in them a strong wish to learn to read. That wish soon caught on with the others too. They quickly rounded up a few old spelling-books, and nothing would do but that I should hold a Sabbath school. I agreed, and so I gave up my Sundays to teaching these dear fellow-slaves to read. Neither of them knew his letters when I arrived. Some of the slaves from the neighboring farms heard what was going on and took advantage of this little chance to learn to read as well. It was understood among everyone who came that there must be as little show about it as possible. We had to keep our religious masters at St. Michael's from finding out that, instead of spending the Sabbath wrestling, boxing, and drinking whisky, we were trying to learn to read the will of God; for they would far rather see us busy with those degrading sports than see us acting like intelligent, moral, accountable human beings. My blood boils when I think of the bloody way that Messrs. Wright Fairbanks and Garrison West, both class-leaders, came rushing in on us along with many others, armed with sticks and stones, and broke up our innocent little Sabbath school at St. Michael's — all of them calling themselves Christians, humble followers of the Lord Jesus Christ! But here I am wandering off the subject again.

I held my Sabbath school at the home of a free colored man whose name I think it unwise to give; for if it came out, it could land him in serious trouble, even though the crime of holding the school was committed ten years ago. At one point I had more than forty students, and the right kind too — people who genuinely wanted to learn. They were of every age, though mostly grown men and women. I look back on those Sundays with a joy I cannot put into words. They were great days for my soul. Teaching my dear fellow-slaves was the sweetest task I have ever been blessed with. We loved one another, and parting from them at the close of the Sabbath was a heavy burden indeed. When I think that these precious souls are today locked up in the prison-house of slavery, my feelings get the better of me, and I am almost ready to ask, "Does a righteous God rule the universe? And what is he holding the thunders in his right hand for, if not to strike down the oppressor and rescue the plundered from the hand of the plunderer?" These dear souls did not come to Sabbath school because it was the popular thing to do, and I did not teach because it was respectable to be so engaged. Every minute they spent in that school, they were liable to be hauled off and given thirty-nine lashes. They came because they wanted to learn. Their minds had been starved by their cruel masters and shut up in mental darkness. I taught them because it was the delight of my soul to be doing something that looked like bettering the condition of my race. I kept the school running nearly the whole year I lived with Mr. Freeland; and besides the Sabbath school, I gave up three evenings a week through the winter to teaching the slaves at home. And I have the happiness of knowing that several of those who came to Sabbath school did learn to read, and that at least one is now free through my doing.

The year went by smoothly. It felt only about half as long as the year before it. I came through it without a single blow landing on me. I will give Mr. Freeland the credit of being the best master I ever had, _until I became my own master._ Still, I owe some of the ease of that year to the company of my fellow-slaves. They were splendid people — they had loving hearts, yes, but courageous ones too. We were bound and tied together. I loved them with a love stronger than anything I have felt since. People sometimes claim that we slaves do not love or trust one another. To that I can answer that I never loved or trusted any group of people more than my fellow-slaves, and above all those I lived with at Mr. Freeland’s. I believe we would have died for each other. We never set out to do anything of importance without talking it over together first. We never acted alone. We were one — as much in our moods and temperaments as in the shared hardships our condition as slaves forced upon us.

When the year 1834 came to a close, Mr. Freeland once again rented me from my master for the year 1835. But by then I was starting to want to live _upon free land_ as much as _with Freeland;_ and so I was no longer satisfied to stay with him or with any other slaveholder. As the year opened, I began getting myself ready for one final struggle that would settle my fate one way or the other. Everything in me pointed upward. I was fast becoming a man, and year after year had slipped past with me still a slave. These thoughts stirred me — I had to do something. So I made up my mind that 1835 would not pass without my making some attempt to win my freedom. But I was not willing to carry that resolve alone. My fellow-slaves were dear to me. I wanted them in on this life-giving decision with me. So, very carefully, I started early to feel out their views and feelings about their situation, and to fill their minds with thoughts of freedom. I threw myself into working out ways and means for our escape, and meanwhile I took every fitting chance to drive home to them the gross fraud and cruelty of slavery. I went to Henry first, then John, then the others. In every one of them I found a warm heart and a noble spirit. They were ready to listen, and ready to act once a workable plan came along. That was exactly what I wanted. I told them how little manhood we would have if we let ourselves stay enslaved without at least one brave try at freedom. We met often, talked it over again and again, shared our hopes and our fears, and went over the difficulties — real and imagined — that we would have to face. At times we nearly gave up and tried to make peace with our wretched lot; at other times we were firm and unbending in our resolve to go. Whenever we proposed a plan, somebody flinched — the odds were terrifying. Our route was blocked with the heaviest obstacles; and even if we reached the end of it, our right to be free was still in doubt — we were still liable to be hauled back into bondage. We could see no place on this side of the ocean where we would be free. We knew nothing about Canada. Our notion of the north reached no farther than New York; and the thought of going there only to be forever hounded by the dreadful chance of being returned to slavery — and the certainty of being treated ten times worse than before — was truly horrible, and not easy to shake off. Sometimes it looked like this to us: at every gate we had to pass, a watchman; at every ferry, a guard; on every bridge, a sentinel; and in every wood, a patrol. We were boxed in on every side. There stood the difficulties, real or imagined — the good we hoped for, and the evil we wanted to escape. On one side stood slavery, a hard fact, glaring down on us in horror, its robes already soaked red with the blood of millions and at that very moment greedily feeding on our own flesh. On the other side, far away in the dim distance, under the wavering light of the north star, behind some rugged hill or snow-covered mountain, stood a doubtful freedom — half frozen — beckoning us to come and share what it had. That alone was sometimes enough to make us waver; but when we let ourselves picture the road, we were often horror-struck. On either side of it we saw grim death taking the most ghastly forms. One moment it was starvation, driving us to eat our own flesh; the next we were fighting the waves and drowning; the next we were overtaken and ripped apart by the fangs of the terrible bloodhound. We were stung by scorpions, chased by wild beasts, bitten by snakes, and at last, after nearly reaching the longed-for place — after swimming rivers, fighting off wild beasts, sleeping in the woods, suffering hunger and nakedness — we were caught by our pursuers, and as we fought back, we were shot dead on the spot! That picture, I tell you, sometimes filled us with dread, and made us
“rather bear those ills we had, Than fly to others, that we knew not of.”

When we finally settled on the firm decision to run away, we risked more than Patrick Henry did when he chose liberty or death. For us, liberty was doubtful at best, and death almost certain if we failed. As for me, I would take death over hopeless bondage.

Sandy, one of our group, dropped out of the plan, but kept cheering us on. That left our company as Henry Harris, John Harris, Henry Bailey, Charles Roberts, and me. Henry Bailey was my uncle and belonged to my master. Charles had married my aunt; he belonged to my master’s father-in-law, Mr. William Hamilton.

The plan we eventually settled on was this: take a large canoe belonging to Mr. Hamilton and, on the Saturday night just before the Easter holidays, paddle straight up the Chesapeake Bay. Once we reached the head of the bay — seventy or eighty miles from where we lived — we meant to set the canoe loose and follow the north star until we had passed beyond the borders of Maryland. We chose the water route because it made us less likely to be suspected as runaways; we were hoping to pass for fishermen. If we went by land instead, we would face interruptions of nearly every kind. Anyone with a white face who felt like it could stop us and put us through questioning.
The week before the day we meant to leave, I wrote out several protections, one for each of us. As near as I can recall, they read in the following words, that is to say:—
“This is to certify that I, the undersigned, have given the bearer, my servant, full liberty to go to Baltimore, and spend the Easter holidays. Written with mine own hand, &c., 1835.
“WILLIAM HAMILTON, “Near St. Michael’s, in Talbot county, Maryland.”
We were not actually heading for Baltimore; but in going up the bay we were heading toward Baltimore, and these protections were only meant to shield us while we were out on the water.

As the day of our departure came closer, our anxiety grew sharper and sharper. For us it really was a matter of life and death. The full strength of our resolve was about to be put to the test. During this time I worked hard at clearing up every difficulty, settling every doubt, chasing off every fear, and filling everyone with the firmness we would need to pull it off; I assured them that half the battle was won the instant we made our move; that we had talked long enough; that we were ready to go now; that if not now, then never; and that if we did not mean to move now, we might as well fold our arms, sit down, and admit we were fit for nothing but slavery. None of us was prepared to admit that. Every man held steady; and at our last meeting we pledged ourselves once more, in the most solemn way, that when the appointed time came we would certainly set out in search of freedom. This was the middle of the week, at the end of which we were to be gone. We went off, as usual, to our separate fields, but our hearts were pounding with thoughts of our truly dangerous undertaking. We did our best to hide what we were feeling, and I think we managed quite well.

After a painful wait, Saturday morning arrived — the morning whose night was to see us go. I greeted it with joy, whatever sadness it might also bring. Friday night I never slept. I was probably more on edge than the others, because by everyone’s agreement I was at the head of the whole thing. The weight of success or failure rested heavily on me. The glory of one and the disgrace of the other were both mine. Those first two hours of the morning were like nothing I had ever lived through before, and I hope never to live through again. Early on, we went out to the field as usual. We were spreading manure; and suddenly, in the middle of the work, I was swept by a feeling I cannot describe, and in the fullness of it I turned to Sandy, who was nearby, and said, “We are betrayed!” “Well,” he answered, “that very thought has just struck me too.” We said nothing more. I have never been more sure of anything in my life.

The horn sounded as it always did, and we came up from the field to the house for breakfast. I went through the motions more than out of any appetite that morning. Just as I reached the house, looking out toward the lane gate, I saw four white men together with two colored men. The white men were on horseback, and the colored men walked along behind, looking as if they were tied. I watched them for a few moments until they came up to our lane gate. There they stopped and tied the colored men to the gate-post. I still was not certain what was going on. A few moments later, Mr. Hamilton came riding in at a speed that showed how worked up he was. He came to the door and asked whether Master William was in. He was told Master William was at the barn. Without getting off his horse, Mr. Hamilton rode up to the barn at an extraordinary pace. Shortly afterward he and Mr. Freeland came back to the house together. By now the three constables had ridden up; in great haste they dismounted, tied their horses, and met Master William and Mr. Hamilton as they returned from the barn; and after talking a while, they all walked up to the kitchen door. No one was in the kitchen but John and me. Henry and Sandy were still up at the barn. Mr. Freeland put his head in at the door and called me by name, saying there were some gentlemen at the door who wanted to see me. I stepped to the door and asked what they wanted. At once they grabbed me and, without explaining a thing, tied me — binding my hands tightly together. I demanded to know what was going on. At last they said they had heard I had been in a “scrape,” that I was to be questioned in front of my master, and that if what they had heard turned out to be false, I would not be harmed.

Within a few moments they managed to tie John. Then they turned to Henry, who had come back by now, and ordered him to cross his hands. “I won’t!” said Henry firmly, showing he was ready to face whatever came of refusing. “Won’t you?” said Tom Graham, the constable. “No, I won’t!” said Henry, even more forcefully. At that, two of the constables drew their gleaming pistols and swore by their Creator that they would make him cross his hands or kill him. Each one cocked his pistol and, with his finger on the trigger, walked up to Henry, telling him as he came that if he did not cross his hands they would blow his damned heart out. “Shoot me, shoot me!” said Henry; “you can’t kill me but once. Shoot, shoot — and be damned! _I won’t be tied!_” He said this in a tone of loud defiance; and at the same instant, with a motion as fast as lightning, he knocked the pistols out of both constables’ hands with a single sweep of his arm. The moment he did, everyone fell on him, and after beating him for a while they finally overpowered him and got him tied.

During the struggle, somehow — I don’t know how — I managed to get my pass out and slip it into the fire without anyone seeing. Now we were all tied; and just as we were about to be taken off to the Easton jail, Betsy Freeland, William Freeland’s mother, came to the door with her hands full of biscuits and shared them out between Henry and John. Then she unloaded a speech on us, which ran roughly like this — turning to me, she said, “_You devil! You yellow devil!_ it was you that put it into the heads of Henry and John to run away. But for you, you long-legged mulatto devil! Henry nor John would never have thought of such a thing.” I said nothing in reply, and was hurried off at once toward St. Michael’s. Only a moment before the scuffle with Henry, Mr. Hamilton had pointed out that they ought to search for the protections he had heard Frederick had written for himself and the rest. But just as he was about to act on the idea, he was needed to help tie Henry, and the commotion of the struggle made them either forget it or decide it was too risky, under the circumstances, to carry out the search. So we had not yet been convicted of meaning to run away.

When we were about halfway to St. Michael’s, while the constables who had us in their charge were looking ahead, Henry asked me what he should do with his pass. I told him to eat it along with his biscuit and admit to nothing; and we passed the word down the line, “_Own nothing;_” and “_Own nothing!_” we all agreed. Our trust in one another had not been shaken at all. We were resolved to win or lose together — just as much after disaster had struck us as before. We were ready now for anything. That morning we were to be dragged fifteen miles behind horses and then locked up in the Easton jail. When we reached St. Michael’s, we went through a kind of examination. Every one of us denied that we had ever meant to run away. We did this more to draw out the evidence against us than from any hope of escaping being sold; for, as I have said, we were resigned to that. The truth was, we cared very little where we ended up, so long as we went together. Our biggest worry was being separated. We dreaded that more than anything this side of death. We learned that the evidence against us rested on the testimony of one person; our master would not say who it was, but among ourselves we reached a unanimous conclusion about who the informant had to be. We were sent off to the jail at Easton. When we got there, we were handed over to the sheriff, Mr. Joseph Graham, who put us in jail. Henry, John, and I were placed together in one room — Charles and Henry Bailey in another. Their aim in splitting us up was to keep us from acting together.

We had scarcely been in jail twenty minutes when a swarm of slave traders and their agents poured in to look us over and find out whether we were for sale. I had never laid eyes on such a crew before! I felt hemmed in by a pack of fiends straight out of hell. A band of pirates never looked more like their father, the devil. They laughed and grinned over us, saying, “Ah, my boys! we have got you, haven’t we?” And after taunting us in all sorts of ways, they went over us one by one, sizing up our worth. They had the gall to ask us whether we wouldn’t like to have them for our masters. We gave them no answer and let them figure it out however they could. Then they would curse and swear at us, telling us they could knock the devil out of us in no time at all, if only they had us in their hands.

While in jail, we found ourselves in far more comfortable quarters than we had braced ourselves for. We did not get much to eat, and what we got was not very good; but we had a clean, decent room, and from its windows we could see what was happening out in the street — far better than if we had been thrown into one of the dark, damp cells. All in all, we got along quite well as far as the jail and its keeper were concerned. The moment the holidays ended, against everything we had expected, Mr. Hamilton and Mr. Freeland came up to Easton and took Charles, the two Henrys, and John out of jail and carried them home, leaving me there alone. I took this separation to be a final one. It hurt me more than anything else in the whole affair. I would have faced anything rather than separation. I figured they had talked it over and decided that, since I was the whole cause of the others wanting to run, it was unfair to let the innocent suffer along with the guilty; and so they had resolved to take the others home and sell me, as a warning to the rest who stayed behind. I owe it to the noble Henry to say that he seemed almost as unwilling to leave the prison as he had been to leave home to come to it. But we knew that, if we were sold, we would very likely be separated; and since he was already in their hands, he decided to go home quietly.

Now I was left to whatever fate held for me. I was utterly alone, inside the walls of a stone prison. Only a few days earlier I had been brimming with hope. I had expected to be safe by now in a land of freedom; instead I was wrapped in gloom, sunk to the very bottom of despair. I thought any chance of freedom was gone for good. They kept me like this for about a week, and at the end of it Captain Auld, my master, to my surprise and complete astonishment, came up and took me out, meaning to send me off into Alabama with a gentleman he knew. But for some reason or other he did not send me to Alabama after all; he decided instead to send me back to Baltimore, to live once again with his brother Hugh and to learn a trade.

So, after being away for three years and one month, I was allowed once more to come back to my old home in Baltimore. My master sent me off because there was a very strong prejudice against me in the community, and he was afraid I might be killed.

A few weeks after I got to Baltimore, Master Hugh hired me out to Mr. William Gardner, a large ship-builder on Fell’s Point. I was sent there to learn how to calk. As it turned out, though, the place was a very poor one for getting that done. That spring Mr. Gardner was busy building two big man-of-war brigs, supposedly for the Mexican government. The vessels had to be launched in July of that year, and if they weren’t, Mr. Gardner stood to lose a large sum; so when I arrived, everything was a rush. There was no time to teach anyone anything. Every man simply did what he already knew how to do. When I entered the shipyard, Mr. Gardner’s orders to me were to do whatever the carpenters told me to do. That put me at the beck and call of about seventy-five men. I was to treat all of them as my masters. Their word was to be my law. My position was about as trying as could be. There were times when I needed a dozen pairs of hands. I would be called in a dozen directions in the space of a single minute. Three or four voices would hit my ears at once. It went like this — “Fred., come help me to cant this timber here.”—“Fred., come carry this timber yonder.”—“Fred., bring that roller here.”—“Fred., go get a fresh can of water.”—“Fred., come help saw off the end of this timber.”—“Fred., go quick, and get the crowbar.”—“Fred., hold on the end of this fall.”—“Fred., go to the blacksmith’s shop, and get a new punch.”—“Hurra, Fred! run and bring me a cold chisel.”—“I say, Fred., bear a hand, and get up a fire as quick as lightning under that steam-box.”—“Halloo, nigger! come, turn this grindstone.”—“Come, come! move, move! and _bowse_ this timber forward.”—“I say, darky, blast your eyes, why don’t you heat up some pitch?”—“Halloo! halloo! halloo!” (Three voices at the same time.) “Come here!—Go there!—Hold on where you are! Damn you, if you move, I’ll knock your brains out!”

This was my schooling for eight months, and I might have stayed longer if not for a truly horrible fight I had with four of the white apprentices, in which my left eye was nearly knocked out and I was savagely beaten in other ways. Here is how it came about. Until shortly after I arrived, white and black ship-carpenters worked right next to each other, and nobody seemed to find anything wrong with it. Everyone seemed quite satisfied. Many of the black carpenters were free men. Things seemed to be going along fine. Then all at once the white carpenters quit work and announced they would not work alongside free colored workmen. The reason they gave was that, if free colored carpenters were encouraged, they would soon take over the trade entirely, and poor white men would be thrown out of work. So they felt obliged to put a stop to it right away. And, taking advantage of Mr. Gardner’s tight spot, they walked off the job, swearing they would not work another minute unless he fired his black carpenters. Now, even though this did not target me on paper, it certainly hit me in practice. My fellow-apprentices soon started to feel it was beneath them to work with me. They began putting on airs and talking about the “niggers” taking over the country, saying we all ought to be killed; and, egged on by the journeymen, they set out to make my life as miserable as they could, bullying me around and sometimes hitting me. I, of course, kept the vow I had made after the fight with Mr. Covey, and I hit back, whatever the consequences; and as long as I could keep them from ganging up, I did fine, because I could whip the whole lot of them one at a time. Eventually, though, they joined forces and came at me armed with sticks, stones, and heavy handspikes. One came at me from the front with half a brick. There was one on each side of me, and one behind me. While I was dealing with the ones in front and on either side, the one behind ran up with the handspike and gave me a heavy blow on the head. It stunned me. I went down, and at that they all rushed me and started beating me with their fists. I let them lay into me for a while, gathering my strength. Then in an instant I gave a sudden heave and rose to my hands and knees. Just as I did, one of them landed a powerful kick in my left eye with his heavy boot. My eyeball felt as if it had burst. When they saw my eye shut and badly swollen, they backed off. With that, I grabbed up the handspike and for a moment chased after them. But here the carpenters stepped in, and I figured I might as well give it up. There was no standing my ground against so many. All of this happened in full view of no fewer than fifty white ship-carpenters, and not one of them put in a friendly word; instead some shouted, “Kill the damned nigger! Kill him! kill him! He struck a white person.” I saw that my only chance to live was to run. I got away without another blow landing, but only barely; for to strike a white man means death under Lynch law — and that was the law in Mr. Gardner’s ship-yard, and very nearly the only law anywhere outside it as well.

I went straight home and told Master Hugh the story of how I had been wronged; and I am glad to say of him that, irreligious as he was, his conduct was heavenly compared with how his brother Thomas had behaved in a similar situation. He listened closely as I laid out the events that led up to the brutal attack, and he showed plainly how furious it made him. The heart of my once over-kind mistress melted into pity again. My swollen-shut eye and blood-covered face brought her to tears. She pulled up a chair beside me, washed the blood from my face, and, with a mother’s tenderness, bound up my head, laying a thin slice of fresh beef over the wounded eye. Seeing kindness once more from this, my once affectionate old mistress, was almost worth all my suffering. Master Hugh was greatly enraged. He let his feelings out by pouring curses on the heads of those who had done it. As soon as I had recovered a little from my bruises, he took me with him to Esquire Watson’s on Bond Street to see what could be done about it. Mr. Watson asked who had witnessed the assault. Master Hugh told him it had been done at midday in Mr. Gardner’s ship-yard, where a large crowd of men were at work. “As to that,” he said, “the deed was done, and there was no question who did it.” Mr. Watson’s answer was that he could do nothing in the case unless some white man came forward to testify. He could issue no warrant on my word alone. Even if I had been killed in front of a thousand colored people, their combined testimony would not have been enough to arrest a single one of the murderers. Master Hugh, for once, was forced to admit that this state of things was too bad. Naturally, it proved impossible to find any white man willing to volunteer his testimony for me and against the white young men. Even those who may have felt for me were not prepared to do it. It took a kind of courage they did not have; for at just that time, the smallest show of humanity toward a colored person was branded as abolitionism, and that label exposed anyone who bore it to terrible dangers. The rallying cries of the bloody-minded in that region and in those days were, “Damn the abolitionists!” and “Damn the niggers!” Nothing was done, and probably nothing would have been done even if I had been killed. Such was, and such still is, the state of things in the Christian city of Baltimore.

Master Hugh, finding he could get no justice, refused to let me go back to Mr. Gardner. He kept me with him, and his wife tended my wound until I was nursed back to health. He then put me into the ship-yard where he was foreman, working for Mr. Walter Price. There I was set to calking right away, and very soon picked up the knack of handling my mallet and irons. Within a year of leaving Mr. Gardner’s, I was able to command the highest wages paid to the most experienced calkers. By then I was worth something to my master. I was bringing him in six or seven dollars a week. Sometimes I brought him nine dollars a week — my wages came to a dollar and a half a day. Once I had learned how to calk, I went out and found my own work, struck my own bargains, and collected the money I earned. My road grew much smoother than before; my life was now much more comfortable. When I could find no calking work, I did nothing. During those idle stretches, the old longings about freedom would come creeping back over me. While I worked for Mr. Gardner, I was kept in such a constant whirl of commotion that I could think of almost nothing but staying alive; and in thinking of my life, I nearly forgot my liberty. I have noticed this throughout my time in slavery — that whenever my situation got better, it did not make me more content; it only sharpened my craving to be free and set me to plotting ways of gaining my freedom. I have found that, to make a slave contented, you must first make him thoughtless. You have to darken his moral and mental sight and, as far as you can, wipe out his power to reason. He must be unable to spot any contradiction in slavery; he must be made to feel that slavery is right; and he can only be brought to that point once he has stopped being a man.

I was now earning, as I have said, a dollar and fifty cents a day. I made the contract for it; I did the work; it was paid to me; it was rightfully mine — yet every single Saturday night I was forced to hand over every last cent of it to Master Hugh. And why? Not because he earned it, not because he had any part in earning it, not because I owed it to him, nor because he had the faintest shadow of a right to it; but purely because he had the power to make me give it up. The right of the grim-faced pirate on the high seas is exactly the same.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Now I reach the part of my life when I planned, and at last carried out, my escape from slavery. Before I describe any of the particular circumstances, though, I think I should say plainly that I do not intend to lay out every fact connected with what happened. My reasons will be clear from the following. First, if I gave a detailed account of everything, it is not just possible but quite likely that other people would be dragged into the most awkward and dangerous trouble. Second, such an account would surely make slaveholders far more watchful than they have ever been before — and that watchfulness would, of course, slam shut a door through which some dear fellow slave might have slipped free of his galling chains. I deeply regret that I am forced to hold back anything important about my experience in slavery. It would genuinely please me, and would add a great deal to the interest of my story, if I were free to satisfy the curiosity I know many people feel by stating every fact about my lucky escape. But I have to deny myself that pleasure, and deny the curious the satisfaction such an account would give them. I would rather suffer under the worst accusations that spiteful men might invent than clear my own name and, by doing so, risk closing even the narrowest path by which a fellow slave might free himself from the chains and shackles of slavery.

I have never liked the very public way that some of our friends out west have run what they call the _underground railroad_ — which, by their own open announcements, has in my view become emphatically the _upperground railroad._ I honor those good men and women for their brave daring, and I applaud them for willingly inviting bloody persecution by openly admitting that they help slaves escape. Still, I can see very little good coming from such a course, either for them or for the slaves getting away. On the other hand, I am certain that these open declarations do real harm to the slaves left behind who are still hoping to escape. They do nothing to enlighten the slave, while they do a great deal to enlighten the master. They prod him into closer watchfulness and increase his power to recapture his slave. We owe something to the slave south of the line as well as to those north of it, and while we help the latter toward freedom, we ought to be careful to do nothing likely to keep the former from getting out. I would keep the merciless slaveholder utterly in the dark about how the slave gets away. I would let him imagine himself ringed by countless invisible tormentors, always ready to snatch his trembling prey out of his hellish grip. Let him grope his way in the dark; let a darkness as deep as his crime hang over him; and let him feel that with every step he takes hunting the fleeing slave, he runs the terrifying risk of having his hot brains knocked out by some unseen force. Let us give the tyrant no help; let us not hold up the lamp that lets him follow the footprints of our fleeing brother. But enough of this. I will now set down the facts about my escape that I alone am responsible for, and for which no one but me can be made to suffer.

Early in 1838 I grew very restless. I could see no reason why, at the close of each week, I should pour the earnings of my labor into my master's pocket. When I handed him my weekly wages, he would count the money, look me in the face with the fierceness of a robber, and ask, “Is this all?” Nothing short of the last cent satisfied him. Now and then, though, when I brought him six dollars, he would hand me back six cents to encourage me. It had the opposite effect. I took it as a kind of admission that the whole sum was rightfully mine. The fact that he gave me any part of my wages proved, to my mind, that he himself believed I was entitled to all of them. I always felt worse for taking anything, because I feared that handing me a few cents eased his conscience and let him imagine himself a fairly honorable sort of robber. My discontent kept growing. I was always watching for a way out, and finding no direct one, I decided to try to hire my own time, in order to save up money to fund my escape. In the spring of 1838, when Master Thomas came to Baltimore to buy his spring goods, I seized the chance and asked him to let me hire my time. He refused without a moment's hesitation and told me this was just another scheme for escaping. He said I could go nowhere he could not reach me, and that if I ran off he would spare no effort to catch me. He urged me to settle down and obey. He told me that if I wanted to be happy I must make no plans for the future. He said that if I behaved properly he would take care of me. In short, he advised me to be completely thoughtless about the future and tried to teach me to depend on him alone for happiness. He seemed to grasp fully how necessary it was to shut down my mind in order to keep me content in slavery. But in spite of him, and even in spite of myself, I kept thinking — thinking about the injustice of my enslavement and about the means of escape.

About two months later I went to Master Hugh and asked for the privilege of hiring my time. He had no idea I had already asked Master Thomas and been turned down. He too seemed inclined to refuse at first, but after thinking it over he granted the privilege and set these terms: I could have all my own time, make my own contracts with whoever hired me, and find my own work; and in exchange for that freedom I had to pay him three dollars at the end of every week and supply my own calking tools, board, and clothing. My board cost two and a half dollars a week. That, plus the wear and tear on clothes and calking tools, brought my regular expenses to about six dollars a week. I had to come up with that amount or give up the privilege of hiring my time. Rain or shine, work or no work, the money had to appear at the end of each week, or I lost my privilege. As anyone can see, the arrangement strongly favored my master. It freed him from any need to keep an eye on me. His money was guaranteed. He got all the benefits of slaveholding with none of its troubles, while I bore all the troubles of a slave and carried all the worry and anxiety of a free man besides. I found it a hard bargain. But hard as it was, I thought it better than the old way of getting by. Being allowed to shoulder a free man's responsibilities was a step toward freedom, and I was determined to hang on to it. I threw myself into making money. I was willing to work nights as well as days, and through tireless effort and industry I earned enough to cover my expenses and put a little money aside every week. I went on like this from May until August. Then Master Hugh refused to let me hire my time any longer. His reason was that one Saturday night I had failed to pay him for my week's time. The failure happened because I went to a camp meeting about ten miles from Baltimore. During the week I had arranged with a group of young friends to leave Baltimore for the camp ground early Saturday evening, and since my employer kept me late, I could not get down to Master Hugh's without letting the company down. I knew Master Hugh had no special need of the money that night. So I decided to go to the camp meeting and pay him the three dollars when I got back.
