I stayed at the camp meeting one day longer than I had planned when I set out. But the moment I returned I went to him to pay what he reckoned he was owed. I found him furious; he could barely hold his anger in. He said he had half a mind to give me a hard whipping. He demanded to know how I dared leave the city without asking his permission. I told him I hired my time, and as long as I paid him the price he asked for it, I did not see that I was bound to ask him when and where I could go. That answer upset him, and after thinking it over for a few moments, he turned to me and said I would hire my time no longer — the next thing he knew, I would be running away. On that same excuse, he told me to bring my tools and clothing home at once. I did, but instead of looking for work, as I used to do before I hired my time, I spent the entire week without doing a single stroke of work. I did it out of spite. Saturday night he came to me as usual for my week's wages. I told him I had no wages; I had done no work that week. At that point we nearly came to blows. He raved and swore he would get hold of me. I did not say a single word, but I was resolved that if he laid a hand on me it would be blow for blow. He did not strike me, but said that from then on he would keep me in steady work himself. I thought it all over the next day, Sunday, and finally settled on the third of September as the day I would make a second try at securing my freedom. That gave me three weeks to prepare for the journey. Early Monday morning, before Master Hugh had a chance to line up any work for me, I went out and got a job from Mr. Butler at his ship-yard near the drawbridge, on what is called the City Block — which made it unnecessary for him to find work for me. At the end of the week I brought him between eight and nine dollars. He seemed very pleased and asked why I had not done the same the week before. He had no idea what my plans were. My point in working steadily was to clear away any suspicion he might have that I meant to run, and I succeeded perfectly. I suppose he believed I had never been more content with my situation than during the very weeks I was plotting my escape. The second week went by, and again I handed him my full wages; he was so pleased that he gave me twenty-five cents — a fairly large sum for a slaveholder to give a slave — and told me to put it to good use. I said I would.

On the surface things really did go smoothly, but underneath there was turmoil. I cannot describe how I felt as the day I had chosen to leave drew near. I had a number of warmhearted friends in Baltimore — friends I loved almost as much as my own life — and the thought of being parted from them forever was painful beyond words. I believe thousands who now stay would escape from slavery if it were not for the strong ties of affection binding them to their friends. The thought of leaving my friends was by far the most painful thing I had to wrestle with. My love for them was my tender spot, and it shook my resolve more than anything else. Beyond the pain of separation, my dread and fear of failing ran deeper than at my first attempt. The crushing defeat I had suffered then came back to torment me. I was certain that if I failed this time my situation would be hopeless — it would seal my fate as a slave forever. I could not hope to escape with anything less than the harshest punishment and being put beyond any means of escape. It took no vivid imagination to picture the most horrifying scenes I would have to go through if I failed. The wretchedness of slavery and the blessedness of freedom hung before me constantly. For me it was life and death. But I held firm, and as I had resolved, on the third of September, 1838, I left my chains behind and reached New York without the slightest interruption of any kind. How I managed it — what means I used, which direction I traveled, and by what mode of transport — I must leave unexplained, for the reasons I gave earlier.

People have often asked me how I felt when I found myself in a free State. I have never been able to answer in a way that satisfied even me. It was the most intensely exciting moment I have ever known. I imagine I felt the way an unarmed sailor must feel when a friendly warship rescues him from a pirate's pursuit. Writing to a dear friend right after I reached New York, I said I felt like someone who had escaped a den of hungry lions. But this mood soon faded, and I was seized again by a deep sense of insecurity and loneliness. I could still be dragged back and put through all the tortures of slavery. That alone was enough to dampen my enthusiasm. But it was the loneliness that overwhelmed me. There I stood among thousands of people, yet a complete stranger — without home and without friends, surrounded by thousands of my own brethren, children of one common Father, and yet I did not dare reveal my sad condition to a single one of them. I was afraid to speak to anyone, for fear of speaking to the wrong person and falling into the hands of money-loving kidnappers, whose trade was to lie in wait for the breathless fugitive the way the ferocious beasts of the forest lie in wait for their prey. The motto I adopted when I set out from slavery was this — “Trust no man!” In every white man I saw an enemy, and in nearly every colored man I found reason for distrust. It was an agonizing situation, and to understand it one must either live through it or imagine himself in the same place. Let him be a fugitive slave in a strange land — a land handed over as a hunting ground for slaveholders, whose people are kidnappers protected by law, where at every moment he risks being seized by his fellow men the way the hideous crocodile seizes its prey. Let him, I say, put himself in my place — without home or friends, without money or credit, needing shelter and finding no one to give it, needing bread and having no money to buy it — and at the same time let him feel that merciless man-hunters are after him, and that he is wholly in the dark about what to do, where to go, or where to stay; utterly helpless both to defend himself and to escape; surrounded by abundance yet gnawed by terrible hunger; surrounded by houses yet having no home; among fellow men yet feeling as though he were among wild beasts whose hunger to swallow up the trembling, half-starved fugitive is matched only by the greed with which the monsters of the deep swallow the helpless fish they live on. Let him, I say, be put in this most agonizing situation — the situation I was in — and then, and only then, will he fully grasp the hardships of the worn-out, whip-scarred fugitive slave, and know how to feel for him.

Thankfully, I did not stay trapped in that misery for long. The kindness of _Mr. David Ruggles_ rescued me from it — a man whose watchfulness, kindness, and persistence I will never forget. I am glad of the chance to express, as far as words can, the love and gratitude I feel toward him. Mr. Ruggles is now stricken with blindness, and is himself in need of the very kindnesses he was once so eager to perform for others. I had been in New York only a few days when Mr. Ruggles sought me out and very kindly took me to his boarding-house at the corner of Church and Lespenard Streets. At the time Mr. Ruggles was deeply caught up in the famous _Darg_ case, while also looking after a number of other fugitive slaves and working out ways and means for their escape; and though he was watched and hemmed in on nearly every side, he seemed more than a match for his enemies.

Very soon after I came to Mr. Ruggles, he wanted to know where I wished to go, since he thought it unsafe for me to stay in New York. I told him I was a calker and would like to go where I could find work. I considered going to Canada, but he decided against it and in favor of New Bedford, believing I could get work there at my trade. Around this time Anna,[2] my intended wife, arrived; for right after I reached New York I had written to her — despite my homeless, houseless, and helpless condition — telling her of my successful escape and asking her to come on at once. A few days after she arrived, Mr. Ruggles called in the Rev. J. W. C. Pennington, who, in the presence of Mr. Ruggles, Mrs. Michaels, and two or three others, performed the marriage ceremony and gave us a certificate, an exact copy of which follows:—
“This may certify, that I joined together in holy matrimony Frederick Johnson[3] and Anna Murray, as man and wife, in the presence of Mr. David Ruggles and Mrs. Michaels.
“JAMES W. C. PENNINGTON “_New York, Sept_. 15, 1838”
[2] She was free.
[3] I had changed my name from Frederick _Bailey_ to that of _Johnson_.

Once I had this certificate and a five-dollar bill from Mr. Ruggles, I hoisted one part of our baggage, Anna took up the other, and we set off at once to board the steamboat John W. Richmond for Newport, on our way to New Bedford. Mr. Ruggles gave me a letter for a Mr. Shaw in Newport and told me that if my money did not stretch as far as New Bedford, I should stop in Newport and get more help. But when we reached Newport we were so eager to get somewhere safe that, even though we lacked the money for our fare, we decided to take seats in the stage and promise to pay once we got to New Bedford. Two fine gentlemen, residents of New Bedford, encouraged us to do this; I later learned their names were Joseph Ricketson and William C. Taber. They seemed to understand our circumstances at once and gave us such assurances of their goodwill that we felt completely at ease around them.

It was good indeed to meet such friends at such a time. When we reached New Bedford, we were sent to the house of Mr. Nathan Johnson, who received us kindly and gave us a hospitable welcome. Both Mr. and Mrs. Johnson took a deep, warm interest in our well-being. They proved themselves fully worthy of the name abolitionist. When the stage-driver found we could not pay our fare, he kept hold of our baggage as security for the debt. I had only to mention this to Mr. Johnson, and he advanced the money right away.

We now began to feel some sense of safety and to ready ourselves for the duties and responsibilities of a free life. The morning after we arrived in New Bedford, at the breakfast table, the question came up of what name I should go by. The name my mother gave me was “Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey.” I had dropped the two middle names long before I left Maryland, though, so I was generally known as “Frederick Bailey.” I left Baltimore under the name “Stanley.” When I got to New York I changed my name again to “Frederick Johnson,” and thought that would be the last change. But in New Bedford I found I had to change it once more. The reason was that there were so many Johnsons in New Bedford that it was already quite hard to tell them apart. I gave Mr. Johnson the privilege of choosing a name for me, but told him he must not take away the name “Frederick.” I had to keep that, to hold on to a sense of who I was. Mr. Johnson had just been reading the “Lady of the Lake,” and he immediately suggested my name be “Douglass.” From then until now I have been called “Frederick Douglass,” and since I am far better known by that name than by any of the others, I will keep using it as my own.

I was quite disappointed by how things looked in general in New Bedford. The impression I had picked up about the character and condition of northern people turned out to be strangely mistaken. While I was a slave I had oddly imagined that few of the comforts, and almost none of the luxuries, of life were enjoyed in the north compared with what southern slaveholders enjoyed. I probably reached that conclusion from the fact that northern people owned no slaves. I assumed they stood about on a level with the non-slaveholding population of the south. I knew _those_ people were extremely poor, and I had grown used to thinking of their poverty as the inevitable result of their owning no slaves. Somehow I had absorbed the notion that without slaves there could be no wealth and very little refinement. So when I came north, I expected to find a rough, hard-handed, uncultivated population living in the most Spartan simplicity, knowing nothing of the ease, luxury, pomp, and grandeur of southern slaveholders. Given those guesses of mine, anyone who knows what New Bedford looks like can easily imagine how plainly I saw my mistake.

On the afternoon of the day I reached New Bedford, I went down to the wharves to look at the shipping. There I found myself surrounded by the strongest evidence of wealth. Lying at the wharves and riding at anchor in the stream, I saw many ships of the finest design, in the best condition, and of the largest size. To my right and left I was walled in by granite warehouses of enormous size, packed to the brim with the necessities and comforts of life. On top of that, nearly everyone seemed to be at work — but quietly, compared with what I had been used to in Baltimore. There were no loud songs from the men loading and unloading the ships. I heard no deep oaths or horrid curses hurled at the laborer. I saw no men being whipped; everything seemed to run smoothly. Every man appeared to know his job and went at it with a sober yet cheerful seriousness that showed both the deep interest he took in his work and a sense of his own dignity as a man. To me this seemed exceedingly strange. From the wharves I wandered around and through the town, gazing with wonder and admiration at the splendid churches, beautiful houses, and finely tended gardens — all displaying an amount of wealth, comfort, taste, and refinement such as I had never seen anywhere in slaveholding Maryland.

Everything looked clean, new, and beautiful. I saw few or no run-down houses with poverty-stricken people inside; none of the half-naked children and barefoot women I had been used to seeing in Hillsborough, Easton, St. Michael's, and Baltimore. The people looked more capable, stronger, healthier, and happier than those in Maryland. For once I was made glad by the sight of great wealth without being saddened by the sight of great poverty. But the most astonishing — and most interesting — thing to me was the condition of the colored people, many of whom, like me, had fled here as a refuge from the hunters of men. I found many who had not been seven years out of their chains living in finer houses, and plainly enjoying more of the comforts of life, than the average slaveholder in Maryland. I will go so far as to say that my friend Mr. Nathan Johnson — of whom I can say with a grateful heart, “I was hungry, and he gave me meat; I was thirsty, and he gave me drink; I was a stranger, and he took me in” — lived in a neater house, dined at a better table, took, paid for, and read more newspapers, and better understood the moral, religious, and political character of the nation than nine tenths of the slaveholders in Talbot county, Maryland. And yet Mr. Johnson was a working man. His hands were toughened by labor, and so were Mrs. Johnson's. I found the colored people far more spirited than I had expected. Among them I found a determination to protect one another from the blood-thirsty kidnapper at all costs. Soon after I arrived, I was told of an incident that showed this spirit. A colored man and a fugitive slave were on bad terms. The colored man was overheard threatening to tell the fugitive's master where he was. At once a meeting was called among the colored people under the standard notice, “Business of importance!” The would-be betrayer was invited to attend. The people came at the appointed hour and organized the meeting by appointing a very religious old gentleman as president, who, I believe, offered a prayer, after which he addressed the meeting like this: “_Friends, we have got him here, and I would recommend that you young men just take him outside the door, and kill him!_” At that, several of them rushed at him, but they were headed off by some who were more timid, and the betrayer escaped their vengeance and has not been seen in New Bedford since. I believe there have been no more such threats, and if there ever are, I have no doubt death would be the result.

On the third day after I arrived I found work, loading a sloop with a cargo of oil. It was new, dirty, hard work for me, but I went at it with a glad heart and a willing hand. I was now my own master. It was a happy moment whose joy can only be understood by those who have been slaves. It was the first work whose reward was to be entirely my own. There was no Master Hugh standing by, ready to rob me of the money the instant I earned it. I worked that day with a pleasure I had never felt before. I was working for myself and my newly-married wife. To me it was the starting point of a new life. When I finished that job, I went looking for calking work, but prejudice against color ran so strong among the white calkers that they refused to work with me, so of course I could get no employment.[4] Since my trade was of no immediate use to me, I cast off my calking gear and got ready to do any kind of work I could find. Mr. Johnson kindly let me use his sawhorse and saw, and I very soon found plenty to do. No work was too hard for me, none too dirty. I was ready to saw wood, shovel coal, carry wood, sweep chimneys, or roll oil casks — all of which I did for nearly three years in New Bedford before the anti-slavery world had heard of me.
[4] I am told that colored persons can now get employment at calking in New Bedford—a result of anti-slavery effort.

About four months after I came to New Bedford, a young man came to me and asked whether I would like to take the “Liberator.” I told him I would, but having only just escaped from slavery, I said I could not pay for it yet. In the end, though, I did become a subscriber. The paper came, and from week to week I read it with feelings I could not begin to describe. It became my food and my drink. My soul was set on fire. Its sympathy for my brothers in bondage, its scorching condemnations of slaveholders, its honest exposures of slavery, and its powerful attacks on those who upheld the institution sent a thrill of joy through me such as I had never felt before!

I had not been reading the “Liberator” long before I had a fairly clear grasp of the principles, methods, and spirit of the anti-slavery reform. I threw myself into the cause. I could do only a little, but what I could do I did with a joyful heart, and I never felt happier than when I was at an anti-slavery meeting. I rarely had much to say at these meetings, because whatever I wanted to say was said far better by others. But while I was attending an anti-slavery convention at Nantucket, on the 11th of August, 1841, I felt strongly moved to speak, and at the same time I was urged to do so by Mr. William C. Coffin, a gentleman who had heard me speak at the colored people's meeting in New Bedford. It was a heavy burden, and I took it up reluctantly. The truth was, I still felt myself a slave, and the idea of speaking to white people weighed me down. I had spoken only a few moments when I felt a measure of freedom and said what I wanted with considerable ease. From that time until now I have been engaged in pleading the cause of my brethren — with what success, and with what devotion, I leave to those familiar with my work to decide.

chapters.title: Appendix
paragraphs: Now that I have read back over this Narrative, I notice that in several places I have spoken about religion in a tone that might lead readers who do not know my views to assume I oppose all religion. To head off that misunderstanding, I think it best to add this short explanation. Everything I have said against religion I mean to apply strictly to the slaveholding religion of this country, and not at all to Christianity itself; for between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ I see the widest possible difference—so wide that to accept the one as good, pure, and holy is necessarily to reject the other as bad, corrupt, and wicked. To be a friend of the one is to be an enemy of the other. I love the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ, and for that very reason I hate the corrupt, slaveholding, woman-whipping, cradle-robbing, partial, and hypocritical Christianity of this land. In fact, I can see no honest reason for calling the religion of this country Christianity at all. To me it is the worst of all misnamings, the boldest of all frauds, and the grossest of all slanders. There was never a plainer case of “stealing the livery of the court of heaven to serve the devil in.” I am filled with a loathing I cannot put into words when I look at the religious pomp and display around me, set against the horrible contradictions that go with it. Our ministers are men-stealers, our missionaries are woman-whippers, and our church members are cradle-robbers. The man who swings the blood-clotted cowskin all week stands in the pulpit on Sunday and calls himself a minister of the meek and lowly Jesus. The man who robs me of my wages at the end of every week meets me on Sunday morning as a class-leader, to show me the way of life and the path of salvation. The man who sells my sister into prostitution stands forth as the pious champion of purity. The man who calls it a religious duty to read the Bible denies me the right to learn to read the name of the God who made me. The man who is religion's great defender of marriage strips millions of its sacred protection and abandons them to wholesale corruption. The same man who praises the sacredness of the family bond is the one who scatters whole families—tearing apart husbands and wives, parents and children, sisters and brothers—and leaves the cabin empty and the hearth cold. We watch the thief preach against theft and the adulterer preach against adultery. Men are sold to build churches, women sold to support the gospel, and infants sold to buy Bibles for the Poor Heathen—all for the glory of God and the good of souls! The slave auctioneer's bell and the church-going bell ring in time with each other, and the bitter cries of the heartbroken slave are drowned out by the religious shouts of his pious master. Revivals of religion and booms in the slave-trade go forward hand in hand. The slave prison and the church stand close together. The clank of fetters and the rattle of chains in the prison, and the pious psalm and solemn prayer in the church, may be heard at the very same moment. The dealers in the bodies and souls of men set up their auction block in plain sight of the pulpit, and the two help each other along. The dealer hands over his blood-stained gold to support the pulpit, and the pulpit, in return, wraps his hellish trade in the clothing of Christianity. Here religion and robbery are allies—devils dressed in the robes of angels, and hell got up to look like paradise.

“Just God! and these are they, Who minister at thine altar, God of right! Men who their hands, with prayer and blessing, lay On Israel’s ark of light. “What! preach, and kidnap men? Give thanks, and rob thy own afflicted poor? Talk of thy glorious liberty, and then Bolt hard the captive’s door? “What! servants of thy own Merciful Son, who came to seek and save The homeless and the outcast, fettering down The tasked and plundered slave! “Pilate and Herod friends! Chief priests and rulers, as of old, combine! Just God and holy! is that church which lends Strength to the spoiler thine?”

The Christianity of America is one whose followers can be described just as truly as the ancient scribes and Pharisees were: “They bind heavy burdens, and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers. All their works they do for to be seen of men.—They love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, . . . . . . and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi.—But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men; for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in. Ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayers; therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation. Ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.—Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint, and anise, and cumin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith; these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Ye blind guides! which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter; but within, they are full of extortion and excess.—Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness. Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.”

Dark and terrible as this picture is, I hold it to be strictly true of the overwhelming majority of professed Christians in America. They strain at a gnat and swallow a camel. Could anything describe our churches more exactly? They would be appalled at the idea of taking a sheep-stealer into fellowship, and yet they clasp a man-stealer to their communion, and brand me an infidel for finding fault with them over it. They attend to the outward forms of religion with Pharisaical strictness, while neglecting the weightier matters of the law—justice, mercy, and faith. They are always ready to make a sacrifice, but seldom to show mercy. They are the very people described as professing to love the God they have not seen while hating the brother they have seen. They love the heathen on the far side of the globe; they will pray for him, pay money to put a Bible in his hands and send missionaries to instruct him—while they despise and utterly neglect the heathen at their own door.

That, in brief, is my view of the religion of this land; and to avoid any confusion arising from broad terms, by “the religion of this land” I mean the religion revealed in the words, deeds, and actions of those bodies, North and South, that call themselves Christian churches and yet stay in union with slaveholders. It is against religion as these bodies present it that I have felt it my duty to testify.

I will close these remarks by reproducing the following portrait of the religion of the South—which, through communion and fellowship, is also the religion of the North—and which I solemnly affirm is “true to the life,” without caricature or the slightest exaggeration. It is said to have been drawn, several years before the present anti-slavery agitation began, by a Northern Methodist preacher who, while living in the South, had the chance to see slaveholding morals, manners, and piety with his own eyes. “Shall I not visit for these things? saith the Lord. Shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?”
A PARODY

“Come, saints and sinners, hear me tell How pious priests whip Jack and Nell, And women buy and children sell, And preach all sinners down to hell, And sing of heavenly union. “They’ll bleat and baa, dona like goats, Gorge down black sheep, and strain at motes, Array their backs in fine black coats, Then seize their negroes by their throats, And choke, for heavenly union. “They’ll church you if you sip a dram, And damn you if you steal a lamb; Yet rob old Tony, Doll, and Sam, Of human rights, and bread and ham; Kidnapper’s heavenly union. “They’ll loudly talk of Christ’s reward, And bind his image with a cord, And scold, and swing the lash abhorred, And sell their brother in the Lord To handcuffed heavenly union. “They’ll read and sing a sacred song, And make a prayer both loud and long, And teach the right and do the wrong, Hailing the brother, sister throng, With words of heavenly union. “We wonder how such saints can sing, Or praise the Lord upon the wing, Who roar, and scold, and whip, and sting, And to their slaves and mammon cling, In guilty conscience union. “They’ll raise tobacco, corn, and rye, And drive, and thieve, and cheat, and lie, And lay up treasures in the sky, By making switch and cowskin fly, In hope of heavenly union. “They’ll crack old Tony on the skull, And preach and roar like Bashan bull, Or braying ass, of mischief full, Then seize old Jacob by the wool, And pull for heavenly union. “A roaring, ranting, sleek man-thief, Who lived on mutton, veal, and beef, Yet never would afford relief To needy, sable sons of grief, Was big with heavenly union. “‘Love not the world,’ the preacher said, And winked his eye, and shook his head; He seized on Tom, and Dick, and Ned, Cut short their meat, and clothes, and bread, Yet still loved heavenly union. “Another preacher whining spoke Of One whose heart for sinners broke: He tied old Nanny to an oak, And drew the blood at every stroke, And prayed for heavenly union. “Two others oped their iron jaws, And waved their children-stealing paws; There sat their children in gewgaws; By stinting negroes’ backs and maws, They kept up heavenly union. “All good from Jack another takes, And entertains their flirts and rakes, Who dress as sleek as glossy snakes, And cram their mouths with sweetened cakes; And this goes down for union.”

In the sincere and earnest hope that this little book may do something to throw light on the American slave system and to hasten the glad day of deliverance for the millions of my brothers and sisters in bondage—relying faithfully on the power of truth, love, and justice to carry my humble efforts through—and solemnly pledging myself anew to the sacred cause, I sign my name,
FREDERICK DOUGLASS.
LYNN, _Mass., April_ 28, 1845.
